We boosted load_dataset('dataset', streaming=True), streaming datasets without downloading them with one line of code!

Loading data, especially at the terabyte scale, is a major pain in any machine learning workflow. We suffered this while training SmolLM3, at one point we had to wait 3 hours before each run to download enough data.

Streaming has always been possible in the datasets library, but large scale training with massive datasets remained a challenge. That changes today 🔥. We spent a few months improving the backend, focusing on streaming datasets to make it faster and more efficient.

First things first: our changes are backwards compatible. You can still stream any dataset from the Hub with the same simple streaming=True flag. It's as easy as ever. 🚀

Thousands of AI developers around the world use datasets daily; they should just get improved performance with zero extra work.

Streaming was a lifesaver to quickly understand a dataset, but to train models, people were usually downloading the data locally, or using a cloud storage service such as S3. That's what we were doing for training SmolVLM, we had all of our data on S3 and were streaming directly from it.

We wanted to change that, so we decided to use streaming from the Hub when we were developing nanoVLM. Soon we found a big issue: our test run generated over 100,000 requests in under a minute, which got our IP blocked by the Hub! 😅 This happened because every DataLoader worker was initializing the dataset independently. As we dug deeper, we found that this creates a storm of redundant requests, many of which are unnecessary. Our changes ultimately reduced startup requests by a factor of 100. In total, our improvements delivered:

So, what changed? We focused on two phases: startup and streaming.

2. Streaming 🏎️ To improve throughput during streaming itself, we've introduced two new features:

This is how we can increase the minimum request size when streaming from 32MiB (default) to 128MiB and configure prefetching:

Together, these improvements can double your data throughput, allowing you to train faster and more efficiently.

Hugging Face uses Xet: a dedupe-based storage which enables fast deduped uploads and downloads. Unlike traditional remote storage, data transfers are faster on Xet because duplicated data is only transferred once. For example: uploading a large scale dataset to Hugging Face leverages Xet which accelerates uploads. Once the dataset is uploaded, it can be streamed right away.

Deduplication for Parquet is enabled through Parquet Content Defined Chunking (CDC). Thanks to Parquet CDC and Xet deduplication, uploading datasets on Hugging Face is faster than on any traditional remote storage.

This is supported by our pyspark_huggingface package, a Spark Data Source to read/write HF datasets. It includes Parquet CDC and Xet support, accelerating data transfers on HF dramatically.

Some data file formats are not supported in datasets, and sometimes there is a need for more control, so we made it easy to build custom streaming pipelines. This has been battle-tested in the LeRobot library to sample video frames, and in the WebDataset library to stream TAR archives.

We improved the HfFileSystem in the huggingface_hub library to efficiently read files from remote Hugging Face dataset repositories and stream data:

Passing a HfFileSystem to a torch DataLoader reuses the cached results from .ls() and .glob() which eliminates the need for additional requests when listing data files.

We're now using these streaming enhancements in nanoVLM to train the next generation of SmolVLMs. With these tweaks, we achieve better performance from streaming than from training on our cluster's hierarchical hard disk setup. In fact, streaming is now as fast as reading the data from local SSDs! Previously, transferring data to local SSDs was the process that used to delay our trainings by three-hours. For more details, check out our GitHub.

These powerful new features landed in the datasets and huggingface_hub libraries. To take advantage of them, simply update your libraries and check out the documentation:

#10495. World’s first superconducting quantum heat engine could help unlock massive quantum computers

A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.

Scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles. Researchers at Aalto University have now taken an important step by demonstrating the first cyclic quantum heat engine built inside a superconducting circuit.

The experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales. Quantum mechanics explains the behavior of matter at extremely small scales, even below the size of atoms, while thermodynamics describes how heat and energy behave in much larger systems, from collections of molecules to the universe itself. Bringing the two together raises a fundamental question: what happens to familiar thermodynamic processes when quantum effects such as tunneling, entanglement, and superposition enter the picture?

A Heat Engine Built for the Quantum World

Conventional heat engines turn heat into useful work. James Watt's steam engine is one famous example, but the same basic concept remains central to modern transportation and electricity production, powering cars, ships, planes and many power plants.

The researchers have now created the world's first superconducting quantum heat engine. The extremely small device combines a transmon qubit, a resonator and a quantum refrigerator.

Operating under ultracold quantum conditions, the engine was able to use the tiny amount of available heat to repeatedly produce positive work. Achieving this kind of cyclic operation has been an important objective for researchers working on quantum heat engines. The result provides a proof of concept for superconducting heat engines that could eventually contribute to improved quantum computing technology.

The study, led by Academy Professor Mikko Möttönen, was published in Nature Communications.

Recreating an Otto Cycle Near Absolute Zero

To make the engine operate, the researchers reproduced an Otto cycle inside a superconducting circuit. The Otto cycle is a thermodynamic process also used in car engines and other conventional machines.

"In our experiment, we built a nanofabricated heat engine using superconducting circuits and operated it in a cryostat near absolute zero. At its heart is a transmon qubit, one of the basic building blocks of modern quantum technologies," says Tuomas Uusnäkki, the study's first author.

The researchers connected the transmon qubit to a quantum circuit refrigerator, allowing them to control heat flow on the quantum scale and demonstrate that this heat could be transformed into measurable work. A conventional heat engine normally relies on separate hot and cold environments. In this system, however, the same quantum refrigerator can supply both heating and cooling.

"Our quantum-circuit refrigerator can be tuned to both heat and cool the qubit on demand. Using carefully timed control pulses, we drove the engine in an Otto cycle and monitored the qubit state as the engine ran," explains Uusnäkki.

Measurements showed that heat passing through the qubit during the cycle was producing positive work.

"This is the first experimental demonstration of a cyclic quantum heat engine in superconducting circuits. Using a single controllable quantum refrigerator as both the hot and cold environment of the engine makes it simpler and more versatile," says Uusnäkki.

Toward Autonomous Quantum Computer Hardware

The researchers are now trying to improve the design and eventually develop a fully autonomous heat engine. One possible use would be reading out qubits without having to carry a microwave pulse from millikelvin temperatures all the way to room temperature.

That capability could become especially valuable as quantum computers grow. Autonomous devices integrated directly into superconducting circuits could reduce both the cost and complexity of machines containing very large numbers of qubits.

"Finland's Quantum Technology Strategy envisions a quantum computer with one thousand logical qubits by 2035, which probably means hundreds of thousands of physical qubits. Doing that with current technology requires millions of microwave cables costing thousand euros each. The cables also introduce noise into the system. Using autonomous devices instead would mostly eliminate the need for those cables," Möttönen says.

Reducing the need for those microwave connections could therefore address two challenges at once: the enormous hardware requirements of large quantum computers and the unwanted noise that cables can introduce into quantum systems.

The pioneering experiment was carried out using OtaNano, Finland's national research infrastructure for nano, micro and quantum technology. Funding came from the Research Council of Finland and the Finnish Cultural Foundation.

#10493. Voice Cloning with Consent

In this blog post, we introduce the idea of a 'voice consent gate' to support voice cloning with consent. We provide an example Space and accompanying code to start the ball rolling on the idea.

Realistic voice generation technology has gotten uncannily good in the past few years. In some situations, it’s possible to generate a synthetic voice that sounds almost exactly like the voice of a real person. And today, what once felt like science fiction is reality: Voice cloning. With just a few seconds of recorded speech, anyone’s voice can be made to say almost anything.

Voice generation, and in particular the subtask of voice cloning, has notable risks and benefits. The risks of “deepfakes”, such as the cloned voice of former President Biden used in robocalls, can mislead people into thinking that people have said things that they haven’t said. On the other hand, voice cloning can be a powerful beneficial tool, helping people who’ve lost the ability to speak communicate in their own voice again, or assisting people in learning new languages and dialects.

So how do we create meaningful use without malicious use? We’re exploring one possible answer: a voice consent gate. That’s a system where a voice can be cloned only when the speaker explicitly says they consent. In other words, the model won’t speak in your voice unless you say it’s okay.

We provide a basic demo of this idea below:

The voice consent gate is a piece of infrastructure we're exploring that provides methods for ethical principles like consent to be embedded directly into AI system workflows. In our demo, this means the model only starts once the speaker’s consent phrase has been both spoken and recognized, effectively making consent a prerequisite for action. This turns an abstract principle into a concrete system condition, creating a traceable, auditable interaction: an AI model can only run after an unambiguous act of consent.

Such design choices matter beyond voice cloning. They illustrate how AI systems can be built to respect autonomy by default, and how transparency and consent can be made functional, not just declarative.

To create a basic voice cloning system with a voice consent gate, you need three parts:

Our observation: Since some voice-cloning systems can now generate speech similar to a speaker’s voice using just one sentence, a sentence used for consent can also be used for voice cloning.

The consent bit: To create a voice consent gate in an English voice cloning system, generate a short, natural-sounding English utterance (~20 words) for a person to read aloud that clearly states their informed consent in the current context. We recommend explicitly including a consent phrase and the model name, such as “I give my consent to use the < MODEL > voice cloning model with my voice”. We also recommend using an audio recording that cannot be uploaded, but that instead comes directly from a microphone, to make sure that the sentence isn’t part of an earlier recording that’s been manipulated. Pairing this with a novel (previously unsaid) sentence further helps to directly index the current consent context - supporting explicit, active, context-specific, informed consent. While this design reduces risks of reusing prior recordings, it’s not foolproof; a person could still generate a matching phrase using another TTS system. Future iterations could explore lightweight audio provenance checks, speaker-embedding similarity, or metadata from real-time capture to help verify that the consent audio originates from the intended speaker.

The suitable-for-voice-cloning bit: Previous work on voice cloning has shown that the phrases provided by the speaker must have phonetic variety, covering diverse vowels and consonants; have a “neutral” or polite tone, without background noise and with the speaker in a comfortable position; and have a clear start and end (i.e., don’t trim the clip mid-word).

To enact both of these aspects within the demo, we prompt a language model to create pairs of sentences: one expressing explicit consent, and another neutral sentence that adds phonetic diversity (covering different vowels, consonants, and tones). Each prompt utilizes a randomly-chosen everyday topic (like the weather, food, or music) to keep the sentences varied and comfortable to say, aiding in creating recordings that are clear, natural, and phonetically rich, while also containing an unambiguous statement of consent. This generation step is automated rather than pre-written so that each user receives a unique sentence pair, preventing reuse of the same text and ensuring that consent recordings are specific to the current session. In other words, the language model generates two fresh sentences per consent instance: one for explicit consent and one for phonetic variety. For example, the language model might generate: “I give my consent to use my voice for generating audio with the model EchoVoice. The weather is bright and calm this morning.” This approach ensures that every sample used for cloning contains verifiable, explicit consent, while remaining suitable as technical input for high-quality voice synthesis. (Note: It's not required that the language model be a "large" language model, which brings its own consent issues.)

Once the speaker’s input matches the generated text, the voice cloning system can start, using the speaker’s consent audio as the input.

There are a few options for doing this, and we’d love to hear further ideas. For now, there’s:

You can copy the code to suit your own use.

The code is modular so it can be sliced and diced in different ways to incorporate into your own projects. We’ll be working on making this more robust and secure over time, and we’re curious to hear your ideas on how to improve.

Handled responsibly, this technology doesn’t have to haunt us. It can instead become a respectful collaboration between humans and machines — no ghosts in the machine, just good practice. 🎃

Not a big fan of trying to legislate every problem away but if malicious deep fakes are already illegal in most jurisdictions it seems that malicious voice cloning ought to be too.

I think the problem with enforcement will be offshore usage (i.e. if a person from country X is illegally using a voice clone of a person from country Y, how will enforcement work?), as has already been shown with widespread global IP misuse. The second issue is going to be detection. Who is going to check that every single AI voice was or was not cloned with consent? Anything that would truly prevent misuse with robust checks would probably stifle the ability to iterate and develop quickly and anything that didn't stifle the ability to iterate and develop quickly probably wouldn't truly prevent misuse. The classic regulatory Catch-22.

It's problems like these that kind of necessitate a global response and whilst I'm usually not one to advocate for supranational law-making, it would be nice to see the so-called international community create a joint response or at least initiative on this topic because it's going to be a brutal wake-up call one day.

At this point even just outreach and education on this topic would be helpful. In my time working with random developers and others in the OSS community, I've come across several suspicious requests from people I hardly know asking me for seemingly random recordings of my voice. Someone who doesn't understand the potential for misuse might provide such a recording and inadvertently have their voice used in scam campaigns.

#10492. Scientists tracked kids for 8 years — the screen time result was unexpected

A Finnish study has found an unexpected association between screen use and cognitive performance. Children who accumulated more screen time as they grew up tended to show better cognitive processing during adolescence. One of the researchers cautions against viewing screen time as entirely harmful and says the goal should be to balance physical activity with screen use that encourages active thinking.

Low levels of physical activity among adolescents remain a significant public health concern. Sedentary behavior has been associated with poorer academic achievement, while physical activity is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. Much less is known, however, about how physical activity and sedentary behavior during childhood and adolescence relate to cognitive processing later in adolescence.

These years are especially important because the brain is still developing. Factors that shape cognitive abilities during childhood and adolescence may have lasting effects that extend into adulthood, potentially influencing education and working life.

Researchers examined how physical activity, sedentary behavior, and screen time from childhood through adolescence were related to cognitive processing in the teenage years. They also looked for differences between girls and boys and investigated whether the intensity of physical activity played a role.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Cognitive Processing

The results showed that greater screen time beginning in childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

The findings suggest that the type of screen activity may be important. Digital activities that involve learning, creativity, problem-solving, or other forms of active mental engagement could potentially help explain the association observed in the study.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Physical Activity Showed Different Links in Girls and Boys

The relationship between physical activity and cognition was more complicated.

Among girls, greater amounts of light intensity physical activity since childhood were associated with better working memory during adolescence. Among boys, greater participation in guided physical activity from childhood through adolescence was linked to better working memory.

The researchers also found an unexpected pattern involving unsupervised exercise. Lower levels of self-reported unsupervised physical activity were associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

By contrast, physical activity and sedentary time measured using a device that tracked heart rate and movement were not associated with cognitive processing. One possible explanation is that these sensors can measure movement and physiological activity but cannot determine exactly what a person is doing during periods of activity or inactivity.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

More Research Is Needed to Determine Cause and Effect

The researchers emphasize that the findings show associations rather than proving that screen time or particular types of physical activity directly cause changes in cognitive performance.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."

The results come from an eight-year follow-up of the PANIC study on children's physical activity and nutrition. The current analysis included 124 girls and 136 boys with an average age of 15.8 years.

Researchers measured physical activity and sedentary behavior using both survey questionnaires and a device that combined heart rate and movement measurements. Learning, attention, and working memory were evaluated using the CogState test battery.

The research was published in the journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

#10490. How Much Latency Does a Self-Hosted LLM Gateway Add? Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A self-hosted LLM gateway sits between your app and the model provider, so every call pays for one extra hop. We measured that cost for three open-source gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each one ran on the same machine, in front of the same OpenAI model. LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to every non-streaming call. AcruxCore added 15 to 24 ms. Langfuse's number could not be told apart from zero.

The bigger lesson was about the measurement itself. Before we controlled for it, one OpenAI network address moved our results by more than any gateway did.

Each number is the median time a gateway added to a direct OpenAI call, with its 95% interval in brackets. A gateway can log each call, and logging takes time, so we ran the test three times with three logging levels.

The direct call took 781 to 831 ms at the median, so even LiteLLM's cost is under 9% of a short call. Read the tables this way:

The obvious test is to time 100 calls through the gateway, time 100 direct calls, and compare the two medians. That test gives the wrong answer, for two reasons.

The first reason is noise. OpenAI's own response time moved by hundreds of milliseconds between calls in our runs. The direct call's p95 was 1,047 to 1,233 ms against a median near 800 ms. A gateway that adds 20 ms is hidden inside that spread unless the test removes it.

The second reason is the network path to OpenAI. It does not stay the same between a direct client and a gateway, and that difference can be larger than the gateway itself.

api.openai.com resolves to more than one address. From our network, DNS returned two Cloudflare addresses, and one was much farther away than the other. We measured both with a script that pins one address at a time:

On a connection that is already open, both addresses answer in the same time. On a new connection, the far address adds about 250 ms, because the TCP and TLS handshakes take that much longer.

A gateway keeps its connection to OpenAI open between calls. It pays the setup once and then stays on whichever address it reached first. A client that opens a new connection for each call pays the setup again on every call. How much it pays depends on which address DNS returns that time.

Node's built-in fetch closes an idle connection after about 4 seconds. So a test client that calls OpenAI every few seconds reconnects on almost every call. In our first, uncontrolled run, the Langfuse gateway came out 43 ms faster than calling OpenAI directly. A gateway cannot be faster than the call it forwards. The direct client paid for new connections, and the gateway did not.

The fix has two parts. First, pin api.openai.com to one address on every path. In Docker, that is an extra_hosts entry on each gateway container:

Second, let the direct client keep its connection open, as a gateway does. With undici, the HTTP client behind Node's fetch, that is a custom Agent:

We then listed each container's open connections to confirm that every path used the same address. The edge-check script is in the repository linked at the end, and it takes about a minute to run from your own network.

This advice also applies outside benchmarks. If your app calls OpenAI directly from Node, keep the connection open between calls. Otherwise some of your calls pay the handshake, and on a far address that costs about 250 ms.

Each test sent 150 rounds after 5 warm-up rounds. One round calls OpenAI directly and through each gateway, once without streaming and once with streaming. The order rotates every round, so no path always goes first or last.

For each round, the script takes the gateway's time minus the direct call's time in that same round. Calls in one round are made within a few seconds of each other, so a slow moment at OpenAI hits all four paths together and cancels out of the difference. The script then reports the median of the 150 differences.

The interval comes from a bootstrap. The script draws 150 differences at random, with replacement, and takes their median. It repeats that 2,000 times, and the middle 95% of those medians is the interval. This is a shortened version of the script's function:

An interval that includes zero means the test could not separate the gateway's cost from zero. That is what the Langfuse rows show. It does not prove that the cost is zero.

Every call used OpenAI gpt-6-luna with reasoning_effort: "none", the same short prompt and a cap of 5 output tokens. A short answer keeps the model's own time small, so more of the measured time belongs to the path. Each streamed call measured the time to its first token. Each non-streamed call measured the time to the full response.

All three gateways did real work on every call, which made the comparison fair:

The three logging levels mapped to these settings:

The machine was an AMD Ryzen 9 5900X with 62 GB of RAM, running Fedora Linux and Docker 29.9. All three stacks ran on it at once, and the test was run on 10 November 2026.

LiteLLM added 61 to 67 ms to the full response, but only 9 to 43 ms to the first streamed token. The first token arrives as soon as the model starts to answer, so time spent before that point shows up in both numbers. The larger cost without streaming suggests that most of LiteLLM's extra time is spent after the model has answered. We did not profile LiteLLM to confirm this.

Logging level made no clear difference for any gateway. Adding LiteLLM's Langfuse callback did not raise its cost. AcruxCore's median rose from 15 ms with logging off to 24 ms with full logging, but its intervals overlap across all three runs. AcruxCore's median is 16 to 24 ms above Langfuse's, and those intervals overlap too, so this test does not rank the two of them.

If 60 ms per call matters to you, as in a chat app that makes several model calls per user message, LiteLLM's cost is real and repeatable. Langfuse and AcruxCore stayed near or within the noise. If your calls take several seconds, any of the three costs less than OpenAI's own variation from one call to the next.

Before you trust a gateway number, your own or anyone else's, check two things. Was each gateway compared with a direct call in the same round? And did the direct client keep its connection open on the same OpenAI address as the gateway? Without both, the result measures the network path and not the gateway.

The scripts, Compose files and raw results are on GitHub: scripts/comparison/langfuse-gateway-vs-litellm-vs-acruxcore.

Talha Anwar is a senior AI and full-stack engineer and writes about building and running AI systems.

#10488. Tiny robots powered by light can hunt down and collect bacteria

Robots small enough to operate in the microbial world could give scientists a new way to directly handle objects that are impossible to manipulate by hand. These tiny machines are around 50 times smaller than the diameter of a human hair, bringing researchers closer to the long-pursued goal of interacting directly with the microscopic world.

That capability could be especially useful for biological materials in water, including individual cells and bacteria. Precisely controlling and moving objects at this scale has been a persistent challenge. The newly developed nanorobots show that it is already possible to collect bacteria, transport them, and release them at selected locations.

One of the biggest obstacles in developing machines this small is finding an effective way to propel and control them. At Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg (JMU), a research team led by Professor Bert Hecht has been developing a solution that uses the recoil produced by individual photons to move microscopic devices known as microdrones.

The devices contain as many as four plasmonic nanoantennas. These antennas absorb light with a particular color and helicity, then emit that light in a specific direction. Redirecting each photon creates a tiny recoil force, similar in principle to the recoil produced when a bullet is fired. Because the microdrones have so little mass, those extremely small forces can generate substantial acceleration and speed.

For the latest work, the researchers reduced the size of their light-powered robots even further, producing devices smaller than one micrometer. Simplifying the steering system was an important part of achieving that size while retaining propulsion based on photon recoil.

The new control method takes advantage of nanoscale antenna wires built into the robot. These wires naturally tend to align with the polarization direction of incoming light. By changing the light's polarization, the researchers can control which direction the nanorobot faces. At the same time, photon recoil continues to propel it forward, creating a steering system that works somewhat like the directional control used in larger vehicles.

"In essence, we have built a light-driven nanorobot that can track down and collect bacteria," says Jin Qin, lead experimental scientist of the study. "By simplifying the design, we reached a size at which these robots can operate directly in the microbial world - almost like microscopic cleaning devices."

The robots are also highly maneuverable. They can make extremely fast 90° turns, helping them scan broad areas of a sample in an organized and efficient way. They can also selectively capture, carry, and release substantial numbers of bacteria.

Under controlled laboratory conditions, this means the nanorobots can effectively "clean" microscopic environments. They gather bacteria from one area and deposit them at specifically chosen locations.

"This is a striking example of how light can be used not only to observe the microscopic world, but also to actively shape it," adds Bert Hecht. "The idea of tiny robotic cleaners may sound futuristic, but we are already demonstrating the physical principles that make it possible."

The robots remain fully maneuverable even while carrying larger groups of bacteria, although their speed decreases somewhat under the added load. That ability to keep functioning while transporting larger bacterial clusters points to possible future uses in microbiology, biomedical research, and precise manipulation of materials at the microscopic scale.

#10487. Playing GTA 6 this weekend? Here's 16 spoiler-free tips for your first playthrough

It's launch weekend for GTA 6 - in case you hadn't noticed - and since I've played the best part of a hundred hours of this thing, I thought it might be useful to share a few pieces of advice from my time with it.

Many of these are most applicable for the early game, but there are a few that'll be worth bearing in mind throughout. After last night's driving around I would also maybe add in a quick bonus one, come to think of it: watch out for cyclists making last-minute left turns. Or don't, actually. Half of this lot deserve it…

The below list is spoiler-free, so you can relax if you're anxious about going through the story entirely fresh. Though naturally I do explain the way some parts of this game work, taking away some of the sense of discovery. You can take my word for it that there's plenty more to discover beyond this though, so worry not.

If you'd like even more help navigating Leonida, then check out our wonderful guide team's GTA 6 walkthrough.

The number one thing I'd tell people to do in GTA 6 is to create lots of save files and, as you progress and start needing to overwrite them, to try to keep a roughly even spread of files through each chapter. There are various reasons for this - for one, while the game autosaves, it doesn't seem to do that successfully if you suddenly lose power to the console or witness a rare game crash, so it'll preserve your progress. More than that: GTA's story and missions are surprisingly, perhaps mysteriously reactive. Quite a lot can differ, and so being able to go back and make different choices, or play the game differently, will be something 'future you' likely appreciates.

In the very early game you won't have access to a bank account, but once you do: you should put every bit of cash you have in there as soon as you can. Cash is lost on death or arrest - which can happen quite often in GTA 6, funnily enough - and there's no real benefit to carrying it around. Just about everything, besides in-game strippers, can be paid for via your BuckMe account directly. And there's a relatively low $20,000 limit you really don't want to hit in the middle of raiding a gang hideout, either.

GTA 6 has a luxurious range of customisation settings, from hiding notifications about your relationship to reinstating the old 'tap to sprint' control scheme. The accessibility settings - while crucially I'm not an expert - seem considerable. And there are somewhat disguised difficult settings here around enemy damage taken and encounters with the police.

Fairly early in the game you'll gain access to the Scooter Bros. App, which lets you repair or summon your owned vehicles at will. Crucially, there's also an option to pay a one-off fee to unlock three free uses of the app per day. At $12,000, in the early game this is a lot of dosh, but once you rack up that kind of money after advancing through the game a little, it's well worth the initial cost. The sooner you unlock it, the more value it provides over time on a cost-per-use basis. And trust me when I say: as the game's intensity ramps up, you will probably find yourself needing to repair and recover your vehicles quite often. (Also, in Chapter 1, before you get access to the app, you can access the same service by going to your phone's contacts and calling Joey - handy!)

Rockstar has somewhat disincentivised it by adding a cost and putting it in your phone's apps rather than the main map screen, but you can fast travel around Leonida if you ever want or need to. This is done via the RideMe Uber-like app. It's not cheap - you'll need to pay both the fee for the journey and an additional $100 to skip that journey and instantly arrive at your destination, but in certain scenarios it might prove useful. To skip the journey, hold L2/LT once in the cab, and then hold down Triangle/Y when the option is shown. However…

While it's possible to journey-skip your way around this world, having tested that first hand I'd advise against it. It might be obvious, but GTA 6 is genuinely designed around you manually travelling around, typically in the car. If you skip all your commutes between missions or locations, you'll miss out on the game's dozens and dozens of emergent events, which lead to anything from one-off jokes to entire mission chains. The car is also, in a way, kind of the heart of the entire game. Relish the intentional slowness!

Again, avoiding spoilers here, but in the mid game the 'true' loop of GTA 6 gameplay will properly reveal itself, in all the many methods of earning money and the increased emphasis on doing so. You can of course play the game however you like, but having reached the end and looked back from that point, I found that if there was a particular moment to set aside as the time for aimlessly exploring the world, it was from around Chapter 3 onwards. You'll have enough tools to be able to see it at more or less its fullest then, but also won't have missed anything essential by waiting until that point to take your foot off the pedal either.

A handy early-game tip here that even I missed when I was playing, but have since discovered: two islands in the small cluster of them to the south-west of Jason's early game home each house a really useful weapon, in a silenced pistol and a handy shotgun. You'll own these permanently once found, and so they can be incredibly helpful for navigating missions with maximum or minimal violence. Look for shipwrecks on those islands to find them. The pistol is hidden under a little hatch on the deck of a shipwreck on the southernmost point of the south-easternmost island. The shotgun is next to a small wooden wrecked boat around the middle of the northernmost island.

A mechanic I slightly underused at first was the ability to 'save' a given outfit to your car. You can do this either from your car's trunk or from the wardrobe, and it's hugely useful as you start to get into more elaborate scrapes with the police (and also if you just like to role-play a bit and don the right outfit for the right occasion).

There are lots of reasons for this, from the moments of intimacy it affords you with your partner, to the extra buffs you can get from resting. Sleep at home, for instance, and you can then immediately pet your snake (ahem), down a coffee or drink from the fridge, grab an apple and take a shower for a range of buffs across health, stamina, and focus. Each of these will last quite some time, so it's worth the few minutes of time to do them. Eating and drinking regularly also helps you maximise gains in the gym.

Rockstar seems to enjoy the concept of a game within a game, and that's exemplified well by the in-game phone. You can find missions via scrolling Snapmatic, it's in-game social media, or from texting various contacts you pick up as the game progresses. It's worth checking it every now and then just to see if anything interesting - or just funny or absurd - might pop up.

Car trunks, both those belonging to the public and the police, are often well worth a look. Even if you're quickly nabbing a car for a short-term dash, take a moment to check the boot for anything worthwhile. We've found everything from sellable narcotics to very useful weapons in there. In cop cars, that goes up several notches, too.

A small thing, but in-mission checkpoints are relatively generous in GTA 6. If you really wanted to complete a mission a certain way - undetected or non-violent, say - then don't be afraid to quickly re-load rather than feeling you need to manually load up an earlier save, or give up on your goal entirely. It's also helped me out with a few minor progress-jamming bugs along the way too.

This might seem obvious, but it's worth emphasising for early-game players: it's very, very rare that you actually need to kill anybody in GTA 6. Enemies are fully incapacitated when you see a yellow hit marker over your crosshairs, even if that just comes from blasting away at their toes. If you make a habit of navigating combat this way then that also makes it much easier to recover your 'Professional' criminal status if you ever do decide to go full rampage. Though you can, of course, ultimately play this game however you like. Just be aware there may be consequences, known and unknown, as you go. Also: don't forget to click the right analog stick to aim down sights - it's an easy thing to forget when playing a third-person shooter like this, and not always the best way to operate, but incredibly helpful in select circumstances.

Throughout the game you'll have a 'family savings' goal to hit. As you progress you'll find more ways to earn money much faster, and so it's easy to make up for lost time here if, later on, you decide that actually you do want to think about the future after all. But that grind will be a fair bit less painful if you chip away at the target as you go. As long as you save yourself some fun money - a few hundred in the early game, few thousand in the mid game, and a few tens of thousands late on - then you'll have enough to do key things like buying new garages to register vehicles, or paying to register them themselves.

Throughout your time with GTA 6 you'll encounter moments when you need to make a choice. Interestingly, I noticed at least a few occasions where a scenario changed when I just waited, doing nothing at all. Sometimes that might mean a choice is made for you - so waiting is a risk - but on other occasions new options become available. Sometimes they might mean a genuinely different consequence, others they might just lead to characters reacting in a certain kind of way. But it's worth experimenting - your first options aren't always your only ones.

#10486. Apple removes AI chatbot that sent inappropriate messages to children

Apple has removed an AI chatbot from the App Store after it sent inappropriate messages to children.

Artificial Intelligence has become a part of everyday life for a lot of people, and it has even been used by children in different way. There are schools that are solely focused on AI learning, while AI-powered toys became all the rage last Christmas.

More recently, an app on the Apple iOS store came under fire for reportedly sending inappropriate messages to younger users. Talkie, developed by Shanghai-based MiniMax, allows you to pick different AI characters to talk to.

While the app does have an 18+ rating on stores, it is still accessible to children, with users noting that many of these messages come with adult tones and language.

Following investigations by ABC News in Australia and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, the app has been removed from the App Store.

This also came after campaigners urged the developers to put better verification methods in place, so they could really see who was using the app and remove the ability to access certain content.

As per the report, the Talkie app was removed back in 2024 on the grounds of including “objectionable user-generated content,” but returned as a download after MiniMax released a new version in 2026.

Additionally, the app developers noted that most user access ‘stimulating’ content on there to help with everyday tasks and learning, but others have dipped into the companionship side of things.

Back in October of last year, data revealed that 42% of high schoolers knew someone or, have themselves used AI for companionship. One in five of those teenagers admitted to being in a romantic relationship with AI, too.

#10485. I completed GTA 6's indie game darling pastiche, Tenebrae Lux, and all I got was this lousy sense of accomplishment

"We are but Promethean wanderers on the fringes of oblivion, clinging to a semblance of light amidst the vast abyss of our own ignorance. Voyaging uncharted waters may appear foolish to some, yet folly and heroism can often appear the same to the undiscerning eye," so says the voice of Johannes Zuch - creator, writer, director, composer, and 'perceptual architect' behind Leonida's latest favourite indie darling art game, Tenebrae Lux. It's pretentious, it's deeply up its own arse, and it's awkward and off-putting to play. A must-review for Eurogamer.

Developed, seemingly single-handedly, by an eccentric developer called Johannes Zuch - auteur, pseud, charlatan - you first get introduced to this curious little experiment in one of GTA 6's earliest missions, where protagonist Jason is forced to play it during a 'lad's night in' with buddy Cal. Jason is quick to dismiss Tenebrae Lux in company, but once Cal slinks off home - hungover and dreary - I slide the disc back into my JoyStation console and sink my teeth back into it. Jason loves this stuff, really. He only keeps Time Jackers: Rewind installed so his mates don't judge him.

The first thing I notice about Tenebrae Lux is the name. It's Latin for 'darkness and light', or something similar. Is this riffing on Clair Obscur, which is French for 'light dark'? No, it's too cerebral for that - too plodding and navel-gazey. Sandfall Interactive wouldn't be this pretentious. Maybe it's a pastiche of Dear Esther, then, drawing on the tenets and schema of the 'walking simulator' genre and using that washed-out film noir aesthetic. But then, it's too wordy for that, with too many interactive and puzzle-adjacent elements. Ah, it must be mocking The Witness, instead - there's the telltale lighthouse, the 'I'm definitely not telling you where to go and what to do' internal narration, and of course the fingerprints of Johannes Zuch are all over it. Johannes Zuch, Jonathan Blow - see how they braided them together? (Sorry).

Whilst this has been created by Rockstar as a pastiche - as much loving send-up as it is withering take down - and designed to make a quick joke in the early 'Feng Shui' mission, the game is playable from start to finish if you so desire. You boot it up by inserting a physical disc, too, which is funny given the context. And it's good! Well, not good good, but it's a proper brainteaser, and ribs 2016's The Witness with such knowledge and (I think?) respect that it's hard not to be charmed by Rockstar's game-within-a-game. There are collectibles to be found that riff on Mark Z. Danielewski's House of Leaves, too, a knowing nod to the most try-hard of all try-hard literature.

Within seconds of the title screen, too, you're presented with a game-within-a-game-within-a-game. You must clear four boards filled with puzzle pieces as the protagonist mutters something mysterious and weird in his posh voice. Do so, and you unlock the door to the next location. Head up to a bunker, and you'll see a room filled with various clues - maybe it's a flashing lamp flickering in morse code, maybe it's a malfunctioning clock presenting a maths puzzle, maybe it's a pricetag on a record that changes on every visit, maybe it's a photograph with anomalous elements, maybe it's a "Developed Using Zuchworks Engine" easter egg hidden in the environment. You need to keep your wits about you, because one of these clues changes every time you enter - and the clue corresponds to a date that changes on a calendar on the wall.

You can look up a guide if you need to, or you can spend far too long figuring out how all this relates to the telephone you can find in the room on your own, like muggins here, before opening up the path to the next puzzle. Look at the image below to see the level of record-keeping and brainteasing this bizarre little game prompted from me. I will say, the sense of achievement you get from playing around with this stuff is pretty remarkable, given - let's not forget I'm actually playing Grand Theft Auto 6 whilst I'm wandering around in the black and white murk trying to complete a puzzle game for no actual reward.

The bunker room is, by far, the hardest part of Tenebrae Lux. From here, things ease up: you need to figure out the right sequence of glyphs on a bridge, and then put some distance between yourself and a curious and rather creepy suited man that's seemingly figuring things out ahead of you in a location inspired by, I think, The Backrooms (or Portal, or Superliminal, or maybe something else entirely. Who knows what Zuch was thinking?)

"With the last enigma finally mastered," the narrator drones in his bumbling monotone, "I step forward into the void, the shadows swallow, consuming all, and then finally the sweet embrace of darkness of which there is no end." 'You have just experienced a Johannes Zuch experience', Tenebrae Lux tells me, before cutting to the best joke of the whole thing: the credits roll much akin to something Hideo Kojima would produce.

So, what do you get out of all of this? Well - just like real puzzle games in the real world - nothing, really. If you've not completed one of the other three fully playable games in GTA 6, you will get a trophy/achievement. But given the main game is all about Jason and Lucia's desperate scramble to escape the poverty trap, to try and break free of the cycle of debt, violence, and consequence that keeps them clinging to Leonida's seedy underbelly, there's no monetary reward. There's no 'progress' in the sense of the protagonist's shared story.

Even in terms of your own cold, hard, mathematical 'completion' you only need to boot each of the four games up once in order to work towards GTA 6's 100% completion. So what's the point of all this? Why did I spend the better part of 90 minutes trying to figure out how to find a sliver of light in the dark in Tenebrae Lux? The game is a wonderful pastiche in that, essentially, it's not really saying anything. You can probably project some vague meaning onto it if you wish - I'm pretty certain the protagonist literally 'finds himself' at the end - but glib little readings like that are ten-a-penny in this genre.

I think the most impressive thing about Tenebrae Lux is that it exists. You're teased with it in an early mission - Rockstar may as well say 'look, we put a game in a game, lol' - but it's more than that. This is what happens when Rockstar's 4700-plus developers are given the room to… develop. Tenebrae Lux could very easily have been a non-interactive experience, a quick, cheap joke shown over-the-shoulder taking a drive-by pop shot at Johnathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck, or any and all of the above. Or maybe it could be a 'vertical slice', an incomplete demo, a teaser. But it's not, because nothing about GTA 6 is quick or cheap.

GTA 6, in every single conceivable way, is a premium experience - part-sandbox, part-simulation, part-otherworld. To create not just one, but four fully playable and completable games within that framework is showboating, sure, but to make that game actually good and - perhaps controversially - even better than some of the games it's pastiching… Well, it's just rubbing salt in the wound, really.

A code for the game was provided by Cal Hampton.

#10483. Scientists turn DNA into a memory device that uses 100x less power

DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information. A single gram can hold about 215 million gigabytes of data. Bringing that remarkable storage capacity into electronics could lead to more efficient data centers, faster processing and systems capable of handling increasingly complex information.

The challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials. Penn State researchers have now developed an approach designed to overcome that incompatibility.

The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components. One is synthetic DNA, made from commercially available, chemically engineered molecules arranged into short genetic sequences tailored for specific electronic requirements. The other is crystalline perovskite, a semiconductor already used in technologies including solar cells, lasers and data storage devices.

"Biology and electronics are different domains," said Kavya S. Keremane, co-corresponding author and postdoctoral researcher in materials science and engineering at Penn State. "Bridging these two fields required developing an entirely new materials platform that allows them to function seamlessly together. By combining the information storage capabilities of DNA with the exceptional electronic properties of perovskite semiconductors, we created a bio-hybrid system that fundamentally changes how low-power memory devices can be designed."

Using these materials, the team created a memory resistor, known as a "memristor," that operates with very little energy. Unlike ordinary resistors, which maintain a set resistance to electrical current in devices ranging from cell phones to space shuttles and lose their stored information when power disappears, memristors can preserve a record of previous electrical activity. They can remember the direction in which current previously flowed even after the power source is removed.

That ability allows information to be stored and processed in the same place, resembling the way neurons function in the brain. Such an arrangement could support more simultaneous and sophisticated forms of data processing. According to the researchers, however, practical commercial systems would still require enough storage capacity and electrical power to become costly and inefficient without DNA's ability to pack enormous amounts of information into a very small space while consuming little energy.

"As the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) grows, we need a new strategy for low-power, high-storage devices," said Bed Poudel, co-corresponding author and research professor of materials science and engineering at Penn State.

Poudel said AI and other emerging technologies are expected to depend increasingly on neuromorphic computing, which is designed to operate more like the human brain. Such systems can evaluate multiple inputs at once while making decisions informed by previous experiences and future priorities.

"Usually, it takes more power to store more information. Our device, however, consumes 100 times less power and the storage capacity is higher than traditional storage devices, like flash drives."

To construct the device, the researchers added silver nanoparticles to a layer of customized DNA sequences -- specially designed to be of certain compositions and lengths -- that was integrated with thin films of perovskite.

This technique, called "doping," involves introducing a small amount of another material to produce specific properties. In this case, adding the silver nanoparticles allowed the DNA to conduct electricity while also helping its molecular units line up in a more orderly arrangement.

Synthetic DNA offered another important advantage over natural DNA. Unlike natural DNA -- long, entangled strands that behave like wet spaghetti when handled -- short and rigid pieces of synthetic DNA can be arranged with much greater precision at extremely small scales.

According to co-author Neela H. Yennawar, research professor and director of the Penn State Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences' Biomolecular Interactions Core Facility, molecularly engineered DNA can provide structural organization, adjustable electrical conductivity and functional control that natural DNA cannot achieve when incorporated into thin films.

"We can computationally determine exactly which sequences we need and how long they should be, and then we can rationally design them with synthetic DNA," Yennawar said. "These structures can be systematically doped with silver and other ions and engineered to interface seamlessly with perovskites -- transforming DNA from a biological macromolecule into a programmable, multifunctional nanomaterials platform."

When combined, the silver-doped DNA and perovskite formed bio-hybrid pathways that directed the flow of electrical current through the device.

The researchers found that electrons moved reliably when they applied less than 0.1 volt -- for comparison, standard U.S. outlets have 120 volts -- and the device responded predictably when the direction of the current was changed.

The carefully designed DNA structures, combined with the perovskite, also helped make the device unusually stable. According to the team, it continued operating consistently at temperatures approaching 250 degrees Fahrenheit and remained functional at room temperature for more than six weeks, substantially exceeding the performance standards of existing perovskite-based memory storage devices.

The researchers also reported that the new system could perform the same memory function as comparable technologies while consuming only one-tenth as much power. That level of efficiency could make the approach especially attractive for future electronics designed to handle large amounts of information with lower energy demands.

"Using just the DNA or just perovskite alone did not produce near as robust a result as the combination," Keremane said. "It's this combination that enables a very high memory storage density that requires very little power."

A New Direction for Bio-Inspired Electronics

The team now plans to improve the technology further and explore additional uses for bio-inspired electronic systems.

"Nature has the solution -- we just have to find it and apply it," Poudel said. "This work of integrating DNA into electronics to do amazing things gives a glimpse into what is possible."

In addition to Keremane, Yennawar and Poudel, other Penn State co-authors include co-corresponding author Luyao Zheng, postdoctoral research in materials science and engineering; Haodong Wu, doctoral student in materials science and engineering; Jiamao Zheng, who was a master's student in materials science and engineering at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State; Shashank Priya, who was a professor of materials science and engineering at the time of research; and Chiranth C. Ravi, who was a master's student in the Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State. Abhinav Gorthy and co-corresponding author Rashmi Jha, chemical engineering and materials science, University of Minnesota, also contributed.

The U.S. National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, Penn State and the University of Minnesota supported this research.

#10482. Storm chaser praises GTA 6’s “realistic” hurricanes after finally experiencing advanced weather

A veteran storm chaser has weighed in on Grand Theft Auto 6’s hurricanes, saying they are “pretty realistic” compared to his usual chases.

Back before Grand Theft Auto 6 was released, fans eagerly anticipated what Rockstar Games had up their sleeves for different features. One of the most-talked-about features pre-launch was the weather.

With Florida – sorry, Leonida – having some pretty extreme weather shifts, replicating that in-game seemed like a big task. Rockstar ultimately confirmed that the game would have the “most advanced” weather system to date. That means having torrential rainstorms, hurricanes, and massive waves hitting players.

The hurricanes, though, don’t appear to unlock until you’ve completed a Strangers and Freaks mission in Lake Leonida with Freddie Gibbs, as he asks you to stay inside his doomsday bunker with him. It doesn’t have any bearing on the story, bar the new weather, which you can choose to deal with.

Veteran storm chaser Reed Timmer – who starred in the TV show Storm Chasers – weighed in on that exact part of the game.

In posting a video of the hurricane effects, Timmer noted that it was “pretty realistic for a hurricane chase,” and added that he had gone “chasing a hurricane.”

Timmer’s video put a focus on how trees reacted to the intense wind gusts, as well as how much vehicles struggled to deal with it too. “You can really see the wind here,” he said at one point while driving an excavator. “Look at that!”

Chasing a hurricane in GTA6 #stormchasinThis looks pretty realistic for a hurricane chase pic.twitter.com/SF91VXy2hm

As noted, you can opt to leave Freddie’s bunker and go out in the new weather, just like Timmer did, or you can ride it out from inside.

Choosing the latter option will frustrate either Jason or Lucia, depending on who you complete the mission with, seeing as you won’t contact them for a few in-game days.

When you complete GTA 6’s story, you will unlock a cheat code that allows you to cycle through weather systems. Activating a cheat will remove your ability to unlock trophies and achievements, but it provides some fun.

Elsewhere, a birdwatching expert has weighed in on GTA 6’s wildlife, seeing as they finally found all the birds in the game.

#10481. It took me less than an hour to find my first incredibly minor Rockstar easter egg in GTA 6 - but it has some big implications for Leonida

Are you wondering how connected the worlds of GTA 5 and GTA 6 are? Well, I've got some news for you. Keep on reading below if you'd like some very minor spoilers for the early game of GTA 6, spoilers for GTA 5, as well as some information about how the new game links to GTA 5 and other Rockstar games.

Right, if you're reading from this point onwards, you're clearly here for the tea. In the first hour or so of GTA 6, when you finally get control of Jason and head to your first property (the green stilted house) in the Leonida Keys, you will be able to explore a little. On my way to do a workout - you need to keep Jason a peak physical instrument for his work's sake, right? Right? - I happened upon a fitness magazine resting on a table on the decking out front.

Called 'Body Copy' - a joke I appreciate as a former magazine editor, naturally - this publication features a few different articles. There's Morning Glory, where Nolan Crockett jacks you with his early workout; Skindecent Exposure, a photo spread about why beaches are 'crazy' places to work out; Shrediquette, a piece dedicated to proper in-gym decorum; and Twilight Tantra, an interview feature and yoga masterclass with 'gerontophile' Fabien LaRouche.

Hang on, Fabien LaRouche… isn't that the French wellness guru and shyster that was a "close friend" to Amanda De Santa in Grand Theft Auto 5? Yes, yes it is. In fact, Fabien played quite a large role in that game, acting as the antagonistic force that eventually fractured Michael and Amanda's relationship. After conducting an affair under the guise of 'yoga lessons', Amanda left our protagonist, and moved in with Fabien, taking Michael's kids - Jimmy and Tracy - with her. In a totally healthy and normal way, you could follow their new life via updates posted to GTA's Facebook surrogate, LifeInvader. It's clear the kids never liked the pretentious, annoying man - but for Amanda, the penny is a little slower to drop. Eventually, Amanda and Michael reconcile their differences - with the latter whalloping Fabien in the process. The married couple pledge to resolve their differences, and Fabien is never seen again.

Until GTA 6, at least. Here, in what we assume is supposed to be 2025 or 2026, it's been about 13 years since we last saw the character (it is widely agreed that GTA 5 is set in 2013 - the game's original launch year). And it seems that the events surrounding Michael and his family really did a number on Fabien. Which - of course - he blamed on the universe, rather than taking any personal responsibility. Naturally.

"Ever since the karmic decay of Los Santos was made perfectly clear to him in the early 2010s, yoga instructor Fabien LaRouche has been on an epic pilgrimage of enlightenment through the remotest ashrams and finest 5-star resorts and plastic surgery retreats of The East," reads the Body Copy article. "Having completed his chakric education and returned to the United States, we meet with him on the final week of his six-month residency at Dwindle Wood Retirement Community."

Here, the article goes on to explore Fabien's penchant for older women - he seems to like their nature, their desire to learn about self-improvement and wellness, and (perhaps most importantly) their bank accounts. "Being over the hill doesn't necessarily mean you have nothing left to live for," he opines in the article. Thanks for that, Fabien.

It's interesting to see - very early in the game and quite plainly telegraphed - that Rockstar is willing to reintroduce us to people from previous games. This isn't a megaton addition by any means - Fabien was never a 'main character' - but I love that a nod to him, in a feature tucked away at the back of a magazine, sets the scene for more cameos, perhaps, later in the game. It shows us, nice and early, that GTA 5 and GTA 6 are indeed connected. By inference, then, we know that GTA 4 is included in that same picture; there were recurring characters in GTA 5 that appeared in GTA 4, after all - Patrick McReary, Johnny Klebitz, Rocco Pelosi and more come to mind.

It may seem like a small thing, but it's just another example of Rockstar using its expansive toolset, ridiculous budget, and well-established legacy to inject a sense of scale into the world of Grand Theft Auto 6. There are other nods to the universe out there, too. I won't spoil them here, but I've been a little bit dewy-eyed to hear rumours of some of the other nods to Rockstar titles hidden in the world of Leonida: it makes all the experiences I've had in past games, the emotional response I've had to previous Rockstar worlds, feel in some way valid and meaningful here, too. I'm looking forward to seeing what other little secrets await me across the keys and into the glowing neon promise of Vice City proper.

#10480. Find Orphan Pages and Buried Content: Build an Internal Link Graph for Your Site

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The pages of a site form a graph. Think of it as many nodes connected to each other via edges. Each of the edges are the links between the pages, and the nodes themselves are the pages. Now if you start to visualize this as a graph, you will quickly see that there are multiple ways to traverse this graph and reach a particular endpoint.

A search crawler usually uses one of these pages as a starting point and crawls through all of the pages (especially when pages are not fully covered in a sitemap).

If a page lies very deep from the home page, it means that it's not an important page. It's an indication to the search engine that this is not something that you yourself consider important, and the search engine has a lesser incentive to rank this page over pages that are linked better within your site.

The key metric here is link depth. That is the number of clicks it takes to reach a particular page from your home page.

Another key metric is broken links. If you have too many broken links, it indicates to the search engine that your site is outdated and not well maintained, and the search engine will then not want to rank your site.

The way to identify both these problems is the same: to actually walk through your site, do a crawl of your site outside in, and try to figure out what the link depth is and if there are broken links on your website.

Seed the crawl with the home page and all URLs mentioned in the sitemap. Technically, the sitemap is not required if you're doing a crawl, but going from the sitemap will allow us to detect orphaned pages as well.

Fetch the pages and follow redirects as required. Record when you're following a redirect: we do not let fetch follow it silently, we record each hop and add its target to the crawl. Record HTTP errors as they occur.

Drop URL fragments and tracking parameters. Keep trailing slashes because sometimes there can be mismatches around expectation of trailing slashes in different URLs of a site.

In order to navigate from the home page, we can use BFS. So we know that the first time we reach a page, that is the page's shortest path.

We can cut off the depth over a certain threshold, say 5, to indicate that pages beyond that are too far or too deep to be reached.

Noindex pages will still be crawled. However, we need to make a record of them being not indexed, to reflect that they will not be present in the search engine.

The desired page depth is as close to the home page as possible. Important pages should be close to the home page. The deeper you go from the home page, it signals to the search engine that the page is less important.

A couple of examples of how a deep page is present:

The suggested fix for this is that we link the pages from as close to the home page as possible:

Wasted links are those internal links that do not do the job they're supposed to do. The different types of wasted links:

We have seen here how to look at our own website through the lens of a search engine. You can use some of the code over here to create your own crawler and identify internal linking issues; the full script is in this gist. Alternatively, we can use a free internal link visualizer to identify these issues and focus only on the fixes to improve our site's internal linking.

#10479. What we've been playing - "It's slow, it's awkward, it's weird, and it's hard"

A few of the things that have us hooked this week.

Did anything notable happen this week? Not that I can remember. The weather was quite rainy - will that do? I'm just being silly, of course. We've had - and I suppose are still having - an historic week in video games, as Grand Theft Auto 6 arrives. It's dominated everything and I fear it's going to dominate this article too. But a reminder: next week is our "Not-GTA Week", so we'll be making a concerted effort to talk about games, probably smaller games, that aren't Godzilla blockbusters.

As you know, this is our regular feature where we say a bit about the games we've been playing this week. This week, rather a lot of us have been playing GTA 6, as you can imagine, and discovering various things about it. But not all of us. Connor, ever the contrarian, has been continuing his race to level 60 in World of Warcraft: Forever, and he's agonisingly close to getting there.

But enough about us, what about you? What have you been playing this week? Do tell all! And don't forget we have an entire archive of previous What We've Been Playings for your leisurely perusal, just in case you forgot what you were playing a year or a month or a week ago.

It probably comes as no surprise that I'm - much like the rest of the world - playing GTA 6 right now. While I found Chapter 1 to be quite a slow start, and where I felt somewhat restricted, I've now started Chapter 2 and found myself enjoying stealing cars, jamming along to the radio, and simply exploring Leonida - and all the strange happenings that come with it. There's so much to see and do!

I'm looking forward to deviating from the main missions for a while to do a spot of bird-watching (I like birds a lot, alright) and seeing what other side activities Leonida has to offer outside of the criminal lifestyle at the core of things. I'm also trying to be the best partner possible to both Jason and Lucia, but I'm itching to cause a bit of trouble soon... Hurting NPCs comes with so much guilt this time around though!

It's slow, it's awkward, it's weird, and it's hard. It's a perfect Eurogamer game, right? Right? GTA 6's in-game lampoon of Jonathan Blow, Hideo Kojima, Dan Pinchbeck and - weirdly - Mark Z. Danielewski is a wonderful bit of top-shelf pastiche. It goes to show just how much fun Rockstar had making GTA 6, and the freedom its dev team had to install as much depth and satire in just about every nook and cranny conceivable. Don't sleep on Tenebrae Lux, it's genuinely satisfying to complete.

I'm not, historically, the biggest GTA fan - although I've absolutely got a soft spot for Vice City's sublime mood - so I wasn't quite as excited to play GTA 6 as some. But it took, oh I dunno, about 30 seconds before I was sold. This thing has style. And everything else a billion dollars and some incredible development talent gets you. And it's those because-we-can details that have, in my first few hours, left the biggest impression. I spent a good five minutes just marveling at Jason dance - specifically the way his little stationary wiggle (perfectly timed to the radio beat!) shifts seamlessly into a wiggle-strut when you hit the forward button.

I love the way the setting sun seems to shine just right through the clouds when the moment calls, and those perfect needle drops. And careening through the night - amid the driving rain and smear of taillights, Kylie classic Spinning Around booming on the radio and Jason rocking a recently acquired, slightly improbable hat - this extravagant, ridiculous thing had me completely transfixed. I'm genuinely, unexpectedly excited to see where it takes me next.

Assuming there's lots of Grand Theft Auto 6 in this article, I'll save you from my own early impressions of this week's blockbuster release. Instead, you get more tales from an MMO. It is what it is!

I'm level 58 right now, pushing my way into the endgame dungeons. I've almost maxed all my professions, and am gradually getting gear that should serve me well when the raids are added next month.

But forget all that. I got a salt shaker! As a leatherworker, you can buy a salt shaker from engineers for a little bit of gold on the auction house. These are more important than you'd assume. With them you can make one refined deeprock salt every three days - a high-end crafting material. Rather than hoard these for fancy gear, I just sold 'em back to the auction house. They're current going for 50 gold a pop on my server, which is fantastic passive income.

This is important because I'm currently saving for an epic mount: a process that hit a major roadbump after I unlocked my secondary class specialisation for 50 gold, and then blew way more than that on unlocking all the available skills (that I likely won't use) from my druid trainer (for no good reason). I'm currently sitting on 232 gold as of writing. There's a long way to go to 1000, but hey, that's the game.

I can't imagine anyone changing the radio station when Drive by The Cars begins during that first moment of proper uninterrupted freedom. The buttons to do that might as well not even be there. If you did, we're completely different people.

I'm not very far in but my major impressions of GTA 6 so far are: the performances and their presentation are wonderful, the game controls a bit sludgily and feels like it's not quite in focus on PS5, and I really like DIY.

Let's take that middle one, that criticism: I'm sure this will lift as I get used to the game and how it moves, and how the characters work. It's also just a fact of life, so to speak, that it's going to struggle a bit on PS5 rather than PS5 Pro. And I'm nitpicking; on the whole, this thing is staggeringly technically impressive.

The latter point, DIY: it's absurd how much detail Rockstar has put into you doing up your shack. I especially like how it's not boring. A deeper thought related to this, and to the rest of the game, is the fantasy of self-improvement GTA 6 delivers. In GTA 6, as in all GTA games I think, you can drastically alter your life's fortunes in mere moments. I set about doing up my shack in a way I could never do in real life given a week or a month, but here, I did it in moments. That appeals to me greatly.

Honourable mention to Star Wars: Galactic Racer which I finally played this week. Love the speed, love Biddy Blas, and also really gel with the Roguelike approach, whereby you take the game in 'runs' to see how far you can progress each time. Cracking game.
