#10426. Building Deep Research: How we Achieved State of the Art

Research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most important applications of AI. Research is a foundational knowledge-work task: collecting, reading, and synthesizing information underpins everything from writing and decision-making to coding itself. Yet human-driven research is constrained by memory, reading speed, and time. AI research agents, by contrast, can process vast amounts of information, synthesize insights instantly, and scale effortlessly. Because of this, research agents are emerging as a top use case for AI today and will soon become a core subcomponent of broader agentic workflows across content generation, coding, sales, and more. In this post, we share the technical and philosophical lessons we’ve learned building a state-of-the-art research agent, and where we believe the field is headed.

The task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling. Building applications on top of rapidly improving models is, however, a modern engineering challenge. How can we design software today that absorbs the performance gains from future model releases?

This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.

We learned this the hard way seven months ago, when we had to abandon our first attempt at deep research and rebuild the entire system from scratch. The first architecture was complicated and sophisticated (we thought this was a good thing), but its assumptions became bottlenecks when the next generation of models arrived.

Over the last seven months, model capabilities have quietly but meaningfully evolved (especially in their tool-calling abilities). This single optimization focus has pushed us from workflows to agents. We believe future models will be trained to solve the current pain points of agent developers. Every model is ultimately consumed by a harness, so models should evolve in service of that harness. We hope to see models improve in high-recall summarization (for context compression), tool-calling reliability, and concision in writing.

Similarly, tools should evolve to support LLMs and widely adopted agent harnesses. The best tools should perform some context engineering on the tool side, abstracted away from the agent. They should return only the most relevant data instead of dumping large volumes of tokens into the context window. As a tool provider, we’ve invested heavily in our advanced search feature, which has context engineering baked in. This in turn lowers hallucinations and latency for the downstream agent processes.

To build agents that improve over time, we followed a few guiding principles:

Long-horizon research tasks expose a fundamental challenge in current agent design: the task of maintaining a clean, optimized context window over time. If curating context is not a task the engineer pays close attention to, the agent is almost destined for failure. The following outlines our thinking around this concept within the deep research domain.

Using Tavily’s Advanced Search is the natural first step to take in overcoming this challenge, in that it abstracts away the processing of raw web content and returns only the most relevant content chunks from each source. In leveraging this functionality, we let Tavily Search do the heavy lifting and allow Tavily Research to reap the benefit, gathering the most valuable content in a latency-efficient manner.

Ensuring that the agent does not overfit to a single research thread is the next step towards an effective context-gathering pipeline. It is in this regard that global state persistence and source deduplication is paramount, and in our case, it helps threefold:

At Tavily, interacting with the web is our bread and butter. Architecting a refined web-retrieval system engineered for deep research was a foundational building block for our deep research agent design as a whole.

Humans research in an inherently unstructured, iterative way. We start by defining the task: what we’re trying to accomplish and what information we need. We next gather data from our sources, extracting the key insights and holding them in short-term memory, letting these distilled thoughts guide our subsequent actions.

This cycle repeats: collect information, distill it, decide what to do next. Only once we’ve gathered enough understanding to produce the final deliverable do we return to the original sources, using them as references to assemble the finished product.

We believe that deep research agents should be designed in a similar manner, in that tool outputs should be distilled into reflections, and only the set of past reflections should be used as context for your tool caller. Similar to humans, it is only at the point when your agent begins to prepare the final deliverable that you must provide the raw information as context, so as to ensure there is no information loss.

This approach differs from traditional context structuring in a ReAct agent-based architecture. Typically, tool calls and outputs are propagated through the tool calling loop, with previously retrieved/generated tokens being persisted in the context window on each subsequent iteration. This pattern can be seen in LangChain’s Open Deep Research agent implementation, and from a token consumption perspective, it can be modeled by the following quadratic series, where n n n is the amount of tokens the tool calling model is invoked with on each tool calling iteration, and m m m is the number of tool calling iterations.

n+2n+3n+⋯+mn  =  n⋅m(m+1)2n + 2n + 3n + \cdots + mn \;=\; n \cdot \frac{m(m+1)}{2}n+2n+3n+⋯+mn=n⋅2m(m+1)​

Contrarily, our proposed method of context engineering removes this token propagation (as the knowledge distillations, even when aggregated, are negligible when compared to the quantity of tokens gathered from web) and can be modeled by the following linear series.

n+n+n+⋯+n  =  nmn + n + n + \cdots + n \;=\; nmn+n+n+⋯+n=nm

When comparing the two approaches, tokens are saved on a per-agent basis by a factor of m+12 \frac{m+1}{2} 2m+1​, and when extrapolating this over a multi-agent system and with consumption at scale, the absolute value of tokens saved becomes even more significant.

Through this methodology, we were able to reduce token consumption by 66% (when compared to Open Deep Research) while achieving SOTA on DeepResearch Bench – the intersection of quality and efficiency in full effect.

Building production-grade agents is a balancing act. We leaned into autonomy to maximize performance and quality, while still meeting strict requirements for latency, cost, and reliability.

LLMs are inherently non-deterministic, and we found that giving them guard-railed freedom to reason and iterate produces the strongest results. Autonomy, when gone wrong, can cause agent behavior to go off track. Tools can be called incorrectly, LLMs can overfit to a subtopic, and expected reasoning patterns may break. No single safeguard will catch all of these issues.

A shift in engineering mindset is required: treat failure modes as core design considerations, not afterthoughts. Simple guardrails like tool-call retries or model cascades help, but proactively anticipating anomalies, reinforcing proper patterns in prompting and edge-case testing is what enables production-grade, long-running agents.

From our experience, it’s better to expose a small, essential toolset to the agent rather than a large, complex one. We were tempted to over-engineer by adding many tools that seemed useful in theory, but in practice this created new failure modes and made it harder for LLMs to consistently choose the right tool and iterate effectively.

We used evals to steer our development process but also recognize their shortcomings. LLM-as-a-judge evals are difficult to trust: current models are non‑deterministic, uninterpretable in their reasoning, and can turn into bottlenecks, especially for long‑running agents where a single experiment can take days to complete.

Rather than optimizing for benchmark scores, we optimized for directional feedback. The core question was always: did this change make the agent more reliable and more useful in practice? Evals became a tool for validating that direction, not the optimization target. Intuition and careful agent‑trace monitoring consistently provided higher‑signal feedback than any single eval score. Overall, the best outcome is rarely the highest numerical score. For production systems, improvements like reduced token usage, reliability, lower latency, and fewer failures are more valuable than a one‑point bump on an eval.

If you’re interested in experiencing the result of these findings in practice, you can sign up for early access to Tavily Research here.

r in the solution is the research insight from previous tool call.

#10424. Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations

Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.

The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.

The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.

Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.

Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.

Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.

The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.

"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.

"You just have to prepare it in the right way.

"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.

"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.

"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."

Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin

Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.

Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.

The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.

Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.

"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."

Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.

To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.

Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.

"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."

The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.

This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.

As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.

The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.

"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.

Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications

The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.

One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.

The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.

Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.

Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.

"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.

"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.

"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.

"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.

These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.

A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed

For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.

By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.

The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.

"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.

"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."

The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.

#10422. Securing FastAPI Applications: JWT Authentication and Rate Limiting with Redis

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Building a modern web API is only half the battle. Ensuring it is secure, resilient, and capable of handling malicious traffic is what separates a hobby project from a production-ready service. When building highly scalable applications, we typically lean on stateless architectures. However, features like token revocation and rate limiting require state.

In this guide, we will explore the architectural concepts behind building a secure API using FastAPI, Redis, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and SlowAPI. We will break down the theory, the tech stack, and the flow of data—without getting bogged down in the code.

Before diving into the architecture, it is crucial to understand the role each tool plays in our security model:

Security starts with how you manage your secrets. The first step in our architectural journey is setting up a configuration file and a local environment file.

Hardcoding secret keys, database URLs, or algorithm types directly into your application is a severe security risk. Instead, we load these from environment variables. The application uses a settings manager to read variables like the Redis host, port, the JWT secret key, the algorithm (typically HS256), and the token expiration time. This ensures that sensitive data stays out of your version control system.

To handle rate limiting and token tracking, we need a connection to Redis. Because FastAPI is inherently asynchronous, we initialize an asynchronous Redis client.

Redis acts as the central state-holder for our API. By using Redis, we ensure that even if our API is running on five different servers behind a load balancer, the rate limits and the token blacklists remain globally synchronized.

Next, we establish the utility functions that handle the cryptographic heavy lifting. This step is divided into two main parts:

Here, we initialize the FastAPI application and attach slowapi.

slowapi needs a way to identify the client making the request. By default, it uses the client's IP address. We attach the limiter to the application state and register an exception handler. This ensures that if a user breaches the rate limit, the API gracefully returns a "429 Too Many Requests" error instead of crashing.

We also set up a dependency that acts as a security guard for our protected routes. This dependency intercepts incoming requests, extracts the token, and decodes it. It then checks Redis to see if the token has been blacklisted (for example, if the user logged out before the token expired). If the token is valid and not blacklisted, the request proceeds; otherwise, a "401 Unauthorized" error is thrown.

The login endpoint is where the magic happens. When a user submits their credentials, the API verifies the username and password. In a production scenario, this involves querying a database; in our example, we verify it against a hardcoded credential.

Once the credentials are validated, the API generates a JWT. To ensure we can invalidate this token later if needed, we store the token in Redis with a time-to-live (TTL) that matches the token's expiration time. Finally, the token is returned to the client, which will store it and send it in the Authorization header of future requests.

Finally, we create a route that requires both authentication and rate limiting.

Before the route's logic even executes, two things happen:

If the client passes both security checks, they are granted access to the highly secure data provided by the route.

To validate this system, you would conceptually walk through several test scenarios. First, you test the login flow with correct and incorrect credentials to ensure tokens are only issued to valid users.

Next, you test the rate limit by rapidly firing requests at the protected route to ensure the "429 Too Many Requests" response triggers. Finally, you test the security guard by trying to access the route with no token, an expired token, and a manually blacklisted token to ensure the API correctly denies access in all scenarios.

Building a secure API requires layering defenses. By combining FastAPI's speed, Redis's fast state management, JWT's stateless authentication, and slowapi's rate-limiting capabilities, you create a system that is both robust and scalable.

While this foundational text explains the core concepts, moving to production requires adding token refresh flows, implementing per-user rate limiting (rather than just IP-based), deploying Redis with high availability, and ensuring your secrets are managed by a secure vault. These practices will ensure your API remains secure as your user base grows.

#10421. Continuous batching from first principles

TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.

If you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency. That's because at the heart of it, all LLMs are just fancy next token predictors. An LLM first processes your entire prompt to produce one new token. Then it keeps adding tokens one by one, each time reading everything that came before, until it decides generation is over.

This generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated. To make these models practical for real-world applications, particularly when serving many users simultaneously, researchers and engineers have developed a range of efficient inference techniques.One of the most impactful optimizations is continuous batching, which attempts to maximize performance by processing multiple conversations in parallel and swapping them out when they are done.

To understand how continuous batching works and why it's so effective in high-load serving scenarios, we'll build up from the fundamentals of how LLMs process tokens.

The attention mechanism is the central piece of how LLMs work. A language model processes text by breaking it down into pieces that we call tokens. We can conceptually think of "tokens" as "words", but sometimes a word might be composed of several tokens. For each token sequence, the network computes a prediction of what the next token should be.

Many operations in the network are token-wise: each token is processed independently, and the output for a given token depends only on that token's content, not on any other tokens in the sequence. Operations like this include layer normalization or matrix multiplication. However, to create connections between words in a sentence, we need operations where tokens can influence each other.

This is where attention comes in. Attention layers are the only place where different tokens interact with each other. Understanding how a network connects tokens together means understanding attention.

Let's see how this works in practice, in the case where there is only one input prompt.

Consider the initial prompt I am sure this project, tokenized as 7 tokens: [, I, am, sure, this, pro, ject]. The , or "Beginning of Sequence", is a special token we add at the start of the prompt to tell the language model that a new conversation starts here.

Each token is represented inside the network with a vector of length d (the hidden dimension). Therefore, the seven incoming tokens form a tensor xxx with shape [1,7,d]\left[1, 7, d \right][1,7,d]. 1 is the number of sequences, or batch size, which is just one in our case. 7 is the sequence length, and d is the hidden dimension, or the size of each token representation. Going forward, we'll use nnn instead of 7 as the sequence length.

Input tensor x x x is then projected by three matrices: the query projection Wq W_q Wq​, the key projection Wk W_k Wk​ and the value projection Wv W_v Wv​. This produces three tensors Q Q Q, K K K and V V V, all of shape [1,n,A] \left[1, n , A \right] [1,n,A], where A A A is the dimension of the attention head. We call them the query, key and value states, respectively. This is represented on the left in the figure below.

Next, tensors Q Q Q and K K K are multiplied together to measure similarity between tokens, producing a tensor of shape [1,n,n] \left[ 1, n , n \right] [1,n,n]. This is why we say that attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length. Computing QKT QK^T QKT requires O(n2d) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 d \right) O(n2d) operations, so the cost is a square of n n n the sequence length. It is represented on the right in the figure above.

We then apply a boolean attention mask to QKT QK^T QKT to control which tokens can interact, as represented in the figure below. In this figure, the attention mask is a causal mask, meaning each token only interacts with tokens that came before it. This follows the intuition that a cause must come before its consequence, hence the name causal mask. The attention mask is crucial because it dictates all token interactions in the network. Set all attention mask values to False and no token will ever interact with another in the whole network. We'll examine attention masks more closely in a few paragraphs.

Finally, after applying the attention mask, we take a token-wise softmax (which is the same as saying a row-wise softmax) and multiply the result by the value projection V V V to get the output of one attention head, of shape [1,n,A] \left[ 1, n , A \right] [1,n,A]. We offer a visual summary of the whole process in the following figure.

We are going to use a lot of attention visualization in this post, so to simplify things, we are going to condense the figure above just a bit.

Why this matters: In continuous batching, Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V can have different numbers of tokens because, as we'll see, we'll be processing different stages (prefill and decode) at the same time. To make it more general, let's say Q Q Q has shape [1,nQ,A] \left[1, n_Q , A \right] [1,nQ​,A], K K K has shape [1,nK,A] \left[ 1, n_K , A \right] [1,nK​,A], and V V V has shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A].

The attention scores QKT QK^T QKT then have shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​], and the attention mask has the same shape since it's applied point-wise to the scores.

After applying the attention mask and row-wise softmax, we multiply by V V V. Since we're multiplying a matrix of shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​] by one of shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A], the inner dimensions must match: nK=nV n_K = n_V nK​=nV​. This means V V V and K K K always have the same length, so we can simplify our visualizations by only showing K K K.Don't worry if this seems abstract: the figures will make it concrete.

Furthermore, since we know that the attention mask is applied to QKT QK^T QKT, we know they have the same shape. Instead of representing the attention scores, we will represent the attention mask in its place. Finally, since Q Q Q, K K K and V V V are direct projections of x x x, no need to represent x x x. This gives the simplified figure where we only represent Q Q Q, K K K and the attention mask:

This representation also underlines how we can read an attention mask.

We read the mask row-by-row, which is the same as reading token-by-token: each row corresponds to one token's attention computation. A green square at position (row i, column j) means True: token j can influence token i. A white square means False: no interaction allowed.

For example, look at the third row for token "am". The "I" column is green, so "I" influences the computation of "am". The "pro" column is white, so "pro" doesn't influence "am" . This is causal masking at work: future tokens can't affect past ones.

The last layer of the model outputs a token prediction for each input token. In our context, generating the continuation of a single prompt, we only care about the next token prediction from the last token. The last token is "ject" in the figure above, and the associated prediction is "will".

The process we just described, where we take an entire input sequence, pass it through multiple attention layers and compute a score for the next token, is called prefill. This is because, as we'll see in a moment, much of the computation we performed can be cached and reused – hence, we are prefilling the cache. Thanks to the use of this cache, sequence generation can proceed using much less compute in a phase called decoding. In the decoding phase, generating one new token will be much faster than the initial full-sequence computation. Let's see why.

To continue generation, we begin a new forward pass, which would naively look like this:

To compute the attention scores of the new token, we still need the key and value projections of the previous tokens. So we need to repeat the matrix multiplication of the old tokens (in grey in the figure above) with Wk W_k Wk​ and Wv W_v Wv​ to retrieve a result that was already computed once before. In other terms, we are wasting compute. Let's see how we can avoid that.

Right off the bat, we notice that the last token does not impact the attention calculation of the other tokens:

This follows the idea of the causal mask: since "will" comes after all previous tokens, it does not change their attention calculation. For text generation, causal attention is by far the most common, so we will focus on that case from now on. Keep in mind that non-causal attention schemes can also be used, especially when dealing with images. Considering we only need the next-token prediction for the "will" token, we can simplify the attention mechanism by only computing the output for this token.

Moreover, we already computed the K K K and V V V states for the tokens "", … , "ject" during the previous forward pass: if they have been stored, we do not need to recompute them again. This is the KV cache: the list of key and value states created during generation. It essentially allows one to reduce the compute cost of generating token n+1 n+1 n+1 from O(n2) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 \right) O(n2) to O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n) by avoiding recomputation of key and value projections, while paying a memory cost of O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n).

In the figure above, only the tokens in white are computed: instead of computing the keys and values for 8 tokens, we compute them for 1. You can see that through KV caching, a lot of compute is saved.You can check this post for more visualizations of KV caching, or this one for a practical implementation example.

Let's be a bit more specific about the cache size, because it's a good opportunity to examine the shapes present in our model. For a model with L \mathcal L L attention layers and H H H attention heads with head dimension A A A, the total cache size needed to store one token will be 2∗L∗AH 2 *\mathcal L * AH 2∗L∗AH with a factor of 2 2 2 to account for both K K K and V V V.For instance, Llama-2-7B with L=32 \mathcal{L}=32 L=32 layers, H=32 H=32 H=32 heads, and A=128 A=128 A=128 requires 2×32×128=8,192 2 \times 32 \times 128 = 8,192 2×32×128=8,192 values per token per layer. With float16 precision, this takes 2AH×2 2AH \times 2 2AH×2 bytes =16 = 16 =16 KB in memory.

KV caching is useful when we want to generate the next token, which is a stage we call decoding. But it can also be useful in the prefill stage, when we process the initial prompt and have many input tokens. Especially when there are large initial prompts that don't fit in GPU memory all at once.

Up till now, we have looked at an example of prefill where we have n=7 n=7 n=7 tokens, but in practice initial prompts can be much longer. For instance, when using Cursor, you can add your repository to the prompt, where it acts as context: this significantly increases the prompt size. In such cases, the memory needed to store the activations for n n n tokens can be larger than the available memory on the GPU. Thus we cannot perform prefill in a single forward pass: we have to split the prefill in chunks. This is called chunked prefill, and it's going to be one of the components needed to enable efficient inference.

Let's pretend that the available memory is very constrained, and that we can only pass m=4 m=4 m=4 tokens per forward pass. If we have an initial prompt with n=7 n = 7 n=7 tokens, we need to split it in ⌈n/m⌉=2 \lceil n /m \rceil = 2 ⌈n/m⌉=2 chunks (rounding up 7/4 = 1.75 to 2). We illustrate the example below using the same n n n and m m m notations:

We can do that thanks to the KV cache. We store the KV states during the first prefill split, and during the second prefill split, we prepend the stored KV states to the new KV states. We also adapt the attention mask accordingly. Visually, it looks like we split the non-chunked prefill in the middle.

The key insight: cached KV states let us process the prompt incrementally without losing information.

Although we showed here an example where we split the prefill into 2 chunks, chunked prefill can be used to split the prefill in any way we want, adapting flexibly to memory constraints.

We are now finally equipped with all the tools we need to understand Continuous Batching.

In our previous examples we have only considered the case of batch size one, i.e. we only generate tokens for one prompt at a time. In the context of evaluation or model serving, we want to generate tokens for a large number of prompts. To increase the throughput, which is the number of tokens generated per second, the best course of action is to generate tokens in parallel for a batch of several prompts.

To batch prompts together, the naive way is to add an axis to both input tensors: token sequence and attention mask. However, this comes with a constraint on the shape of the inputs: we need all prompts to have the same length, because tensors must be rectangular. To achieve this, we usually add padding on the left so the new token prediction always comes from the rightmost token. We also modify the attention mask of each prompt accordingly, as shown below:

where the padding tokens are coloured in orange. Then we can perform the forward pass as we used to, with the added dimension of the batch size. This is called batched generation: efficient for same-length prompts, but wasteful when lengths vary.It is illustrated below, through 4 steps of generation: one prefilling step (at the top) and 3 decoding steps (below each "Forward pass" lines).

where means "End Of Sequence", this is a special token to indicate the model has reached the end of generation for the corresponding sequence.

The drawback of batched generation is that if one prompt finishes generation before the other one by generating an token, all further generated tokens are useless. And this goes on until the longest request of the batch finishes. Of course, we can remove the prompts that have reached an token from the batch and save some compute and memory, but saving resources is not the goal here: throughput is.

Instead of just removing the finished prompt from the batch, we can replace it with a prompt that's waiting for generation. We will call this dynamic scheduling, or dynamic batching. Dynamic scheduling is great to maintain throughput while ensuring any token generated by a forward pass is relevant. But because of the way we batched prompts together, it has a major drawback: we need a lot of padding when swapping prompts. That's because the newly-inserted prompt needs to go through prefill while the other prompts are decoding one token at a time. So there is almost as much padding as there are tokens in the newly-inserted prompt.

The problem becomes even worse when batch size increases and initial prompts are long. The padding cost grows quadratically with both batch size and prompt length. If we have a batch of B B B prompts that are in decoding phase and one finishes, dynamically introducing a prompt of n n n initial tokens in the batch requires (n−1)(B−1) (n-1)(B-1) (n−1)(B−1) padding tokens. For instance, with B=8 B=8 B=8 and n=100 n=100 n=100, we'd need 99×7=693 99 \times 7 = 693 99×7=693 padding tokens!

Furthermore, practical optimizations like CUDA graphs or torch.compile require static tensor shapes. This forces us to pad all prompts to a fixed maximum length, dramatically increasing the padding waste.

At this point, our main problem is padding, which is a consequence of the axis we added to batch sentences together. Thus, the ideal would be to get rid of this axis entirely, a radical rethinking of batching. If we do so, the only way to batch prompts together is to concatenate them:

But we don't want tokens from prompt 0 to interact with the tokens of prompt 1! Luckily for us, we have a way to control how tokens interact with one another: the attention mask. How we do this is displayed below:

Although we use different tints of green to illustrate the different parts of the attention mask, this is still a boolean mask with only greens for True and white for False. This way of batching prompts together is called ragged batching (because sequence lengths are 'ragged' or uneven), and it offers the benefit of added throughput without introducing the need for padding tokens.

In the figure above, we use ragged batching to combine two full prompts together, but we can batch as many as memory allows. The only limit is m m m, the number of tokens we can fit in a batch, with m m m depending on the available memory on the GPU.

Ragged batching is one of the key components of continuous batching. To maximize throughput, we can combine prefill and decoding sequences following an algorithm like this:

Dynamic scheduling is the final piece that contributes to the continuous batching technique: we remove finished prompts from the batch as soon as they are done, and replace them with new chunked prompts that correspond to incoming requests.

This combination of ragged batching and dynamic scheduling is called continuous batching, and it's the technique that powers modern LLM serving systems.

Continuous batching combines three key techniques to maximize throughput in LLM serving:

By removing the batch dimension and using attention masks to control token interactions, continuous batching allows mixing prefill and decode phases in the same batch, dramatically improving efficiency for serving multiple requests. This is why services like ChatGPT can handle thousands of concurrent users efficiently.

In the next article in this series, we make continuous batching much more efficient by introducing asynchronous batching. Read it here!If you'd like to see a deep dive on other continuous batching topics, please let us know in the comments!

Thanks for the article! I'd like to add one note: the primary reason we need chunked prefill isn't the memory constraint (otherwise we could simply solve it with Flash Attention). The more practical reason is that a long prefill blocks all decode requests in the batch. Chunking it lets decode requests make progress between chunks. Moreover, since prefill chunks make the forward pass compute-bound, decode tokens can piggyback on the same batch at nearly zero marginal cost - they're just extra rows in an already large matmul. This turns memory-bound decode-only batches into better-utilized compute-saturating ones. See the SARATHI paper for details.

#10420. AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious

Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).

As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?

New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.

How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness

Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.

"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.

"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."

To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.

Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.

A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness

The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.

However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.

The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.

"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."

Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.

The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.

Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.

Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.

The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.

"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."

#10419. I love YouTube on TV, but we desperately need better watchlist controls

Managing a YouTube watchlist shouldn’t be as frustrating as it is, especially on the most-used app in my life. Google’s premier streaming app has too many issues with resurfacing content; in my opinion, this is now a major problem that needs to be fixed.

Aside from my YouTube watchlist gripes, it’s no secret that moving from a web browser to the TV is ultimately still a frustrating experience.

Lots of things I love about watching videos on my laptop or PC just don’t translate well to when I’m sat on my sofa holding a remote trying to find something to watch after wrapping up for the day. One thing I’m getting annoyed with is how YouTube scales on TV and Android TV boxes because you’re given less choice and arguably poorer recommendations for content due to the constraints in place.

Understandably, you can’t compress the layout too much on a TV as you’re typically sat a few feet away and all aspects of the interface need to be legible. I would still like to tweak it, though, if that were possible.

Maybe we could get proper sections for content, like how Netflix and other streaming platforms offer categorized areas where you can search for “comedy” or “horror”. I’m almost certain that, with Google’s insane investment and massive AI push, where every video is already analyzed hundreds of times, that wouldn’t be too difficult to do.

The problem now is that the sidebar menu is just too broad. Gaming covers basically everything. Then each line of videos accounts for one title, but requires search and previous watch data to populate. I find myself often fighting with recommendations on my TV, whereas on desktop it’s not as much of a problem.

That leads me to my biggest problem with YouTube, and it’s the, frankly, embarrassing watchlist or “Watch later” controls.

I can’t fault that it works, but right now the watchlist function is like something out of the early 2000s due to the lack of flexibility that I touched on above. As my YouTube consumption has increased 20x over the past four or five years, managing what I want to come back to or might have missed the first time around is starting to become a bit of a chore.

I’ve tried using playlists to save things, but things get messy very quickly because of how cumbersome it is to a) create a playlist on TV and b) how playlists are organized by default.

Google TV isn’t perfect, but it’s where I keep my biggest TV and movie watchlist outside of YouTube. Yes, YouTube is mostly for user-generated content, but I would take something as basic as Google TV’s interface baked into YouTube somehow. Add in categorization and auto-clear.

The Watch Later section has become an unwieldy place that I never really want to go unless I desperately have to. I’m constantly losing videos that I hoped to come back to or have an affinity for.

Videos don’t clear automatically, nor do you know when they were added. Yes, I’ll give credit that you can sort by a few options, but that’s the bare minimum. The process of moving things around is slow and takes multiple taps. Watch Later is also hidden compared to other services. It’s under your account, then beneath “Liked videos,” which is below any you may have uploaded yourself.

On a TV, the process is so annoying I just avoid it altogether. You go to the sidebar menu > Library > Watch later. It should be front-and-center on a TV. It’s almost unforgivable in my eyes because even your watch history is given greater prominence. I simply cannot understand that decision.

I’m not always a huge fan of AI being shoehorned into apps and services, but this is one of those areas that has been left to rot for a while and could get a big uplift from adding in a little bit of Gemini. Even if it were just an enhanced search function or more tools for organizing.

With YouTube TV effectively taking over regular broadcast television and being the world’s biggest streaming platform, I’m shocked by how so many areas of the platform remain in a consistently neglected state.

A little bit of spit and polish, and maybe I’ll start using this section again. For now, though, I’ll stick to texting myself links of stuff I want to watch. The ball is in your court, Google.

#10416. People are taking an unapproved weight-loss drug. AI found something surprising

An experimental weight-loss drug that has not yet received regulatory approval is already attracting users willing to obtain unapproved versions online. Now, scientists are using artificial intelligence to investigate their experiences, uncovering unexpected symptom reports that differ from those documented in clinical trials.

The drug, retatrutide, belongs to a new generation of GLP-1 medications designed to help regulate appetite and body weight. Although it remains under investigation and is not approved for use, people are purchasing unapproved formulations that are not intended for human consumption and discussing their experiences on internet forums.

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania analyzed nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments from approximately 40,000 users to investigate these accounts. Their study, published in JAMA Network Open, provides the first systematic examination of potential side effects reported by people claiming to use unapproved retatrutide.

One finding stood out. Among users whose reported symptoms could be classified, increased appetite was the most common complaint. That was particularly unexpected because retatrutide is designed to suppress hunger, and its Phase 2 clinical trials primarily identified digestive problems as the most frequent side effects.

AI Uncovers Unexpected Weight-Loss Drug Reports

"Our goal is to identify hypotheses in online conversations that we could test. AI helps us find recurring patterns in people's self-reports, including experiences that may be missed by conventional drug-safety monitoring," says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS), Director of Penn's Computational Social Listening Lab and senior author of the study.

However, the researchers emphasize that the findings should not be interpreted as proof of previously unknown side effects. Reddit users represent a very different population from clinical trial participants, and their accounts cannot establish whether the drug caused the symptoms they described.

There is also considerable uncertainty about what these individuals are actually taking. Products sold outside regulated medical channels may differ from the genuine experimental medication in their ingredients, purity, and dosage.

"We can't say that retatrutide is causing these symptoms, or even that Reddit users are actually taking genuine retatrutide, since the drug is not legally available, and gray market formulations vary," says Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author of the study.

Rather than confirming new risks, the research offers scientists an opportunity to identify questions that warrant more rigorous investigation.

"This is the first glimpse into the experiences of a population that is otherwise outside conventional drug safety monitoring because they are taking unapproved versions of a drug that has yet to finish clinical trials," says Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS.

How Researchers Analyzed 150,000 Reddit Posts

The project builds on previous research by the University of Pennsylvania team. In that earlier investigation, scientists used large language models (LLMs), the type of artificial intelligence that powers many modern chatbots, to examine more than 400,000 Reddit posts discussing semaglutide and tirzepatide.

That analysis revealed reports of possible side effects, including menstrual irregularities, that may not have been fully documented in clinical trials or official drug safety records.

"We wanted to apply the same methodology to gray-market retatrutide," says Sehgal.

Retatrutide is particularly interesting because it works differently from existing GLP-1 medications. Semaglutide acts on one hormone receptor involved in blood sugar control and appetite regulation, while tirzepatide targets two. Retatrutide activates three receptors, potentially producing a different combination of effects throughout the body.

To investigate what people were experiencing, the researchers used AI to examine nearly 150,000 Reddit posts and comments. They identified approximately 14,000 users who claimed to have personally taken an unapproved version of retatrutide.

The AI systems then extracted descriptions of symptoms that users associated with the medication and translated those descriptions into standardized medical terminology. This allowed researchers to compare reports even when different people used different words to describe similar experiences.

After excluding expected effects such as weight loss and reduced appetite, the team identified 7,823 users who reported at least one symptom that could be medically classified.

"A researcher might be able to examine a few thousand Reddit posts by hand, but looking at nearly 150,000 would be an enormous undertaking," says Sehgal. "AI makes it possible to analyze these conversations at scale, identifying patterns in what people are sharing that would otherwise be difficult to recognize."

The most striking difference involved hunger.

In retatrutide's Phase 2 clinical trials (the drug is currently in Phase 3 trials, the final step before FDA approval), participants most commonly experienced gastrointestinal complaints, including nausea. These effects are familiar concerns with medications that influence appetite and digestion.

But among Reddit users who reported taking unapproved retatrutide, the pattern looked different. Increased appetite emerged as the most frequently described classifiable symptom, despite the substantial weight-loss effects demonstrated in clinical testing.

The researchers also compared the new findings with their earlier analysis of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

Compared with those earlier Reddit reports, discussions involving unapproved retatrutide contained proportionally more mentions of appetite-related changes, sleep disturbances, increased heart rate, and muscle-related symptoms. Reports of nausea and other digestive complaints were proportionally less common.

These differences could reflect how retatrutide interacts with the body. However, they could also result from differences between the groups of people discussing the medications, their other drug use, or the contents of the unapproved products.

"Retatrutide works differently from existing GLP-1 drugs, so it's possible that its effects on the body are different, too," says Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study.

"But the people discussing it on Reddit also may be different," she notes. "Users willing to obtain an unapproved medication on the gray market likely differ from other clinical populations. Some may be taking multiple experimental peptides, and we can't verify exactly what they're taking. We need more research to understand what, if anything, these differences in self-reported symptoms mean."

Can AI Detect Drug Safety Concerns Earlier?

Beyond the findings about retatrutide, the study demonstrates how AI could potentially improve the early detection of drug safety concerns.

Traditional monitoring systems depend heavily on clinical trials, reports submitted to regulators, and information collected by healthcare professionals. People obtaining experimental medications through unapproved channels may not be represented in those systems.

Social media offers another source of information, allowing researchers to identify recurring experiences that might otherwise escape attention. However, these reports must be independently investigated before they can be considered reliable evidence of a drug-related problem.

The Penn team has already seen an example of how this approach can help guide further research.

In their previous investigation of semaglutide and tirzepatide, researchers identified online reports of menstrual irregularities. Those findings subsequently encouraged another scientific team to examine similar symptoms using the FDA's database of reported adverse drug events.

The follow-up study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology, also detected disproportionate reports of certain menstrual changes. Although those findings did not establish causation, they provided additional reasons to investigate the potential connection.

The researchers hope their retatrutide findings will lead to similar independent studies, particularly as the drug advances through clinical development.

"That's what we hope will happen with this study," says Sehgal. "Other researchers can take what we find on Reddit and look for the same patterns in other datasets, using entirely different methods. Whether those signals hold up or not, the goal is to build a better understanding of what people are actually experiencing."

The research was conducted through the University of Pennsylvania's School of Engineering and Applied Science and Perelman School of Medicine. Benjamin Rader of Boston Children's Hospital also contributed as a co-author. Funding was provided in part by the University of Pennsylvania's Penn Medical Communication Research Institute. Tronieri disclosed receiving an investigator-initiated grant from Novo Nordisk on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, along with consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. No conflicts of interest were reported by the other authors.

Materials provided by University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10415. Diffusers welcomes FLUX-2

FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series. It is an entirely new model with a new architecture and pre-training done from scratch! In this post, we discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2, performing inference with it under various setups, and LoRA fine-tuning.

🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a new image generation and editing model.

FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation. Furthermore, it can take multiple images as reference inputs, while producing the final output image. Below, we briefly discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2.

First, instead of two text encoders as in Flux.1, it uses a single text encoder — Mistral Small 3.1. Using a single text encoder greatly simplifies the process of computing prompt embeddings. The pipeline allows for a max_sequence_length of 512. Instead of using a single-layer output for the prompt embedding, FLUX.2 stacks outputs from intermediate layers, which have been known to be more beneficial.

FLUX.2 follows the same general multimodel diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) + parallel DiT architecture as Flux.1. As a refresher, MM-DiT blocks first process the image latents and conditioning text in separate streams, only joining the two together for the attention operation, and are thus referred to as “double-stream” blocks. The parallel blocks then operate on the concatenated image and text streams and can be regarded as “single-stream” blocks.

The key DiT changes from Flux.1 to FLUX.2 are as follows:

Time and guidance information (in the form of AdaLayerNorm-Zero modulation parameters) is shared across all double-stream and single-stream transformer blocks, respectively, rather than having individual modulation parameters for each block as in Flux.1.

None of the layers in the model use bias parameters. In particular, neither the attention nor feedforward (FF) sub-blocks of either transformer block use bias parameters in any of their layers.

In Flux.1, the single-stream transformer blocks fused the attention output projection with the FF output projection. FLUX.2 single-stream blocks also fuse the attention QKV projections with the FF input projection, creating a fully parallel transformer block:

Note that compared to the ViT-22B block depicted above, FLUX.2 uses a SwiGLU-style MLP activation rather than a GELU activation (and also doesn’t use bias parameters).

A larger proportion of the transformer blocks in FLUX.2 are single-stream blocks (8 double-stream blocks to 48 single-stream blocks, compared to 19/38 for Flux.1). This also means that single-stream blocks make up a larger proportion of the DiT parameters: Flux.1[dev]-12B has ~54% of its total parameters in the double-stream blocks, whereas FLUX.2[dev]-32B has ~24% of its parameters in the double-stream blocks (and ~73% in the single-stream blocks).

FLUX.2 uses a larger DiT and Mistral3 Small as its text encoder. When used together without any kind of offloading, the inference takes more than 80GB VRAM. In the following sections, we show how to perform inference with FLUX.2 in more accessible ways, under various system-level constraints.

Before you try out the following code snippets, make sure you have installed diffusers from main and have run hf auth login.

The above code snippet was tested on an H100, and it isn’t sufficient to run inference on it without CPU offloading. With CPU offloading enabled, this setup takes ~62GB to run.

Users who have access to Hopper-series GPUs can take advantage of Flash Attention 3 to speed up inference:

You can check out the supported attention backends (we have many!) here.

Using bitsandbytes, we can load the transformer and text encoder models in 4-bit, allowing owners of 24GB GPUs to use the model locally. You can run this snippet on a GPU with ~20 GB of free VRAM.

Notice that we're using a repository that contains the NF4-quantized versions of the FLUX.2 DiT and the Mistral text encoder.

Due to the modular design of a Diffusers pipeline, we can isolate modules and work with them in sequence. We decouple the text encoder and deploy it to an Inference Endpoint. This helps us with freeing up the VRAM usage for the DiT and VAE only.

⚠️ To use the remote text encoder, you need to have a valid token. If you are already authenticated, no further action is needed.

The example below uses a combination of local and remote inference. Additionally, we quantize the DiT with NF4 quantization through bitsandbytes.

You can run this snippet on a GPU with 18 GB of VRAM:

For GPUs with even lower VRAM, we have group_offloading, which allows GPUs with as little as 8GB of free VRAM to use this model. However, you'll need 32GB of free RAM. Alternatively, if you're willing to sacrifice some speed, you can set low_cpu_mem_usage=True to reduce the RAM requirement to just 10GB.

You can check out other supported quantization backends here and other memory-saving techniques here.

To check how different quantizations affect an image, you can play with the playground below or access it as standlone in the FLUX.2 Quantization experiments Space

FLUX.2 supports using multiple images as inputs, allowing you to use up to 10 images. However, keep in mind that each additional image will require more VRAM. You can reference the images by index (e.g., image 1, image 2) or by natural language (e.g., the kangaroo, the turtle). For optimal results, the best approach is to use a combination of both methods.

FLUX.2 supports advanced prompting techniques like structured JSON prompting, precise hex color control, and multi-reference image editing. Aside for the added control, this also allows for flexibility in changing specific attributes while maintaining others overall the same.For example, let's start with this json as the base schema (taken from the official FLUX.2 prompting guide):

Building up on that, let's turn it into a prompt for a shot of a good old fashion walkman on a carpet (simply pass this prompt to your chosen diffusers inference example from above):

Now, let's change the color of the carpet to a specific teal-blue shade (#367588) and add wired headphones plugged into the walkman:

The carpet color now matches the hex code provided, and the headphones have been with small changes to the overall scene.

Check out the official prompting guide for more examples and details.

Being both a text-to-image and an image-to-image model, FLUX.2 makes the perfect fine-tuning candidate for many use-cases! However, as inference alone takes more than 80GB of VRAM, LoRA fine-tuning is even more challenging to run on consumer GPUs. To squeeze in as much memory saving as we can, we utilize some of the inference optimizations described above for training as well, together with shared memory saving techniques, to substantially reduce memory consumption. To train it, you can use either the diffusers code below or Ostris' AI Toolkit.

We provide both text-to-image and image-to-image training scripts, for the purpose of this blog will focus on a text-to-image training example.

Many of these techniques complement each other and can be used together to reduce memory consumption further. However, some techniques may be mutually exclusive, so be sure to check before launching a training run.

Please make sure to check out the README for prerequisites before starting training.

The left image was generated using the pre-trained FLUX.2 model, and the right image was produced the LoRA.

#10413. MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells

A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.

The engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a new study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.

By directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.

In experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.

"It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," says study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. "

A New Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle

The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.

Most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.

"Currently, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," says Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's new bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself."

The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.

From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot

The new swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.

For that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.

When illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.

The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.

"People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman says. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny."

For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.

They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.

The earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could quickly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.

To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.

"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman says. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells."

Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot

Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.

The researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.

This alignment was important because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.

The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.

By adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.

Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.

The engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.

The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.

With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.

The finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.

Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.

"You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman says. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap."

To test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.

As the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.

Although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.

The researchers now plan to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a new approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.

"Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments."

The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.
