#10398. What Is the Best UI design Tool? 8 Tools Compared by the Job They Do (2026)

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

The ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your users discover first: broken layouts, usability issues that no longer work, and new accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository. In 2026, most frontend teams don't rely on a single tool to do all of that. The best setups involve two layers: a test runner layer that launches the browser and monitors behavior, and a UI testing and review platform that visually checks the outcome and routes changes to the right stakeholders for sign-off.

Even with the right stack, it still relies on what your team needs to catch. Different teams will focus on different points: a QA team trying to automate checkout flows, a design system team defending shared components, and a single developer working on a tight budget will all be somewhere different. This guide is categorized by the job these UI testing tools do, then connects them.

Most "best UI testing tool" lists rank test runners and visual testing platforms against each other as if they were interchangeable. They aren't. UI testing covers four distinct jobs:

Functional testing: Does the UI respond correctly when a user clicks, types, or hovers?

Visual testing: Does the UI still look right across layout, color, typography, and spacing?

Accessibility testing: Can people using keyboards and screen readers use it, and did this change introduce new violations?

Cross-browser and device coverage: Does it work in Safari on mobile, not just Chrome on a developer's laptop?

There are also other levels of UI tests. Unit tests test the logic but don't interact with the UI. End-to-end (E2E) tests represent the full user journey in a browser but are difficult to set up, hard to troubleshoot when the bug is a visual detail, and can't practically test every state. Between the extremes of unit tests and E2E tests, component tests simulate each component's behavior in a real browser using fixed inputs, offering speed closer to unit tests and user-level coverage closer to E2E. Many teams maintain a thin layer of E2E tests for critical journeys, and they have component tests for the dozens of states a component may be in.

These tools are organized by job so you can stack them rather than choose one winner

These platforms sit on top of your test runner. They capture rendered UI, compare it to approved baselines, and give your team a place to review what changed.

Chromatic is a UI testing and review platform made by the Storybook team. It catches visual, interaction, and accessibility bugs in components and pages before they merge, and it gives developers, designers, and product managers one place to review UI changes and sign off. Chromatic's team is the core maintainer of Storybook, which has about 90,000 GitHub stars and 17 million weekly npm downloads, and a Vitest core maintainer on the team built Chromatic's Vitest integration. Chromatic is used by 45 Fortune 100 companies, including GitHub, Shopify, Microsoft, Adobe, the BBC, and monday.com.

Pricing: Free plan with 5,000 snapshots per month (Chrome only), unlimited projects and users. Starter is $179/month for 35,000 snapshots and adds Safari, Firefox, and Edge. Pro is $399/month for 85,000 snapshots. Enterprise is custom, with SSO, SCIM, SLA support, and data retention. TurboSnap snapshots count as 0.2 of a regular snapshot.

Trade-offs: Chromatic is strongest when your UI is built from components. Teams with no component tests can start from Playwright or Cypress E2E tests, but they'll get the most value once components are covered too. Snapshot usage also grows with each browser and viewport you add, so plan coverage before you scale it.

Best for: Design system teams, product teams that want designers and PMs to approve UI changes, React Native teams, and Vitest-first teams that want visual testing without baselines stored in the repo.

Percy is BrowserStack's visual testing platform. It captures screenshots from your existing tests, renders them across browsers and responsive widths, and highlights pixel differences for review.

Strengths: Framework-agnostic SDKs for Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, and Storybook. App Percy covers native mobile apps. The free plan includes 5,000 screenshots per month with unlimited users and projects.

Trade-offs: Percy is page-oriented, and each page rendered in each browser at each width counts as a separate screenshot, so usage climbs quickly with cross-browser coverage. Percy compares feature branches against a base branch, which teams with complex branching should test early. Reviewers see rendered screenshots rather than an inspectable copy of the code under test, so debugging a diff usually means reproducing it locally.

Pricing: Free tier, then paid plans with fixed screenshot allowances and overage.

Best for: Teams already paying for BrowserStack that want visual checks on page-level E2E tests.

Applitools Eyes uses Visual AI to compare screenshots the way a person would, with match levels that can ignore content changes and focus on layout. Its Ultrafast Grid re-renders captured page states across many browser, viewport, and device combinations.

Strengths: Mature AI matching, broad browser and device coverage, Figma and Storybook testing, accessibility testing, and an MCP server. Higher tiers add AI-driven functional testing and plain-English test authoring.

Trade-offs: Applitools is priced and packaged for enterprises. There's a free trial but no free plan, and the Starter plan is $667/month billed annually for 100,000 component checkpoints or 1,000 page checkpoints. Professional and Enterprise are custom-priced.

Best for: Large QA organizations with big cross-browser matrices and budget for a dedicated visual AI platform.

BackstopJS is a free, open-source visual regression testing tool released under the MIT license. You list the URLs, viewports, and CSS selectors to capture in a config file, and BackstopJS renders them in a headless browser through Playwright or Puppeteer, then compares the results against approved reference screenshots. The core workflow runs on three commands: backstop init, backstop test, and backstop approve.

Strengths: Completely free, with no screenshot limits. A built-in browser report shows reference and test images side by side with a visual diff inspector, and changes can be approved from there. Optional Docker rendering keeps screenshots consistent between laptops and CI; Playwright adds Firefox and WebKit, and click, hover, and keypress selectors capture interactive states. JUnit reports plug into existing CI pipelines.

Trade-offs: BackstopJS is self-hosted, so there's no cloud dashboard, shared team review, or pull request status checks out of the box. Reference screenshots are usually committed to your repository, and every page or component state you want to test needs its own URL and scenario in the config. Someone on the team also has to own the setup, CI integration, and maintenance.

Best for: Developers and small teams with no budget who are comfortable running and maintaining their own visual regression setup.

Test runners click, type, and assert. They're free and open source, and every platform above builds on them. On their own, they offer limited visual testing: built-in screenshot assertions store baselines in your repository, rendering can drift between laptops and CI, and designers have no review interface.

Playwright is Microsoft's open-source browser automation framework. It runs tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with auto-waiting, trace viewer debugging and code generation, and supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.

Visual testing: Playwright's toHaveScreenshot assertion compares screenshots against baselines stored in Git. It works, but baselines must be regenerated per operating system, and accepting a change means rerunning with an update flag.

Best for: Teams automating critical user journeys such as sign-up, checkout and login. Pair it with a platform like Chromatic for visual review across real browsers.

Cypress is an open-source testing tool that runs inside the browser, with time-travel debugging that shows the app at each step of a test. It supports both E2E and component testing.

Visual testing: Cypress has no built-in visual comparison and relies on plugins or a platform such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools. Cypress Cloud, its paid service, adds recording, parallelization, flake detection and add-ons for accessibility and UI coverage.

Best for: Frontend developers who want fast feedback and an interactive test runner while they build.

Storybook is the open source workshop for building UI components in isolation. Each story captures one component state, and those stories double as test cases.

Testing features: Interaction tests with play functions and Testing Library, accessibility checks with the a11y addon, and a Vitest integration that runs stories as component tests.

Visual testing: Storybook doesn't diff screenshots on its own. Chromatic, built by the same team, is its visual testing and review layer.

Best for: Design system and component library teams, and any team practicing component-driven development.

Vitest Browser Mode runs component tests in a real browser instead of a simulated DOM, using Playwright or WebdriverIO under the hood.

Visual testing: Vitest's toMatchScreenshot assertion stores screenshots in the repository. For large projects, this can bloat the repo and baselines drift between machines. Chromatic can take Vitest Browser Mode tests with no code changes and run them in a stable cloud environment instead.

Best for: Teams already writing Vitest tests who want them to check how the UI looks without adopting a new framework.

Start from the problem your team is trying to fix:

"Shared component changes keep breaking other teams' screens." Test at the component level with Storybook or Vitest Browser Mode and Chromatic, so the change shows up on the pull request that caused it.

"Our Playwright tests pass, but the layout still breaks in Safari." Functional assertions don't check appearance. Add a visual testing platform that renders in Safari, such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools.

"We turned off screenshot tests because of false alarms." Look for deterministic component states and flake controls such as Chromatic's SteadySnap, or AI matching such as Applitools.

"Designers find UI bugs after release." Choose a platform with a review and approval workflow, and make sign-off a required pull request check.

"AI coding agents keep inventing components." Give agents access to your real component library, for example through Chromatic's hosted MCP, and run every agent-built change through the same UI tests as human code.

"We have no budget." Use Playwright or Vitest screenshot assertions, self-host BackstopJS, or start on the free tiers of Chromatic or Percy.

A practical, well-covered setup for a React web app looks like this:

Unit tests in Vitest for logic and utilities.

Storybook stories or Vitest Browser Mode tests for every meaningful component state, with interaction tests on key components.

Chromatic running visual, interaction and accessibility tests on those components in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge on every pull request, with designers assigned as reviewers.

A thin layer of Playwright E2E tests for sign-up, checkout and other critical journeys, also captured in Chromatic so page-level visual changes go through the same review.

This keeps most UI coverage in fast, deterministic component tests, while E2E tests confirm the journeys that matter most still work end to end.

Playwright is the best free tool for E2E UI testing, and Storybook is the best free tool for testing component states. For visual testing, For visual testing, Chromatic and Percy both offer free tiers of around 5,000 snapshots or screenshots per month, and BackstopJS is free to self-host.

UI testing is the broad practice of checking that an interface works for users, including functional, visual and accessibility checks. Visual testing is one part of it: comparing rendered UI against approved baselines to catch unintended changes in layout, color, typography and spacing.

No. Chromatic was built by the Storybook team, but it also runs visual tests from Vitest Browser Mode, Playwright and Cypress tests, and from React Native Storybook on iOS and Android simulators.

Playwright's toHaveScreenshot covers basic visual checks, but baselines live in your repo, rendering can differ between machines, and there's no review interface for designers. Teams with several reviewers or many browsers usually add a platform on top.

Most teams use both. Component tests cover individual UI states quickly and reliably, while a smaller set of E2E tests confirms that critical user journeys work across the whole app.

#10396. DeepMath: A lightweight math reasoning Agent with smolagents

DeepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Instead of verbose text, the model emits tiny Python snippets for intermediate steps, runs them in a secure sandbox, and folds the results back into its reasoning, reducing errors and output length. The agent is implemented using the smolagents library.

We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:

🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.

⚡ GRPO training improves the agent performance even further, in almost all benchmarks.

👉 Code and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/IntelLabs/DeepMath 👉 Model: https://huggingface.co/Intel/deepmath-v1

Large language models (LLMs) have advanced reasoning capabilities, but mathematical problem-solving remains challenging; chain-of-thought traces can be lengthy and prone to arithmetic mistakes. Recent works[^1][^2] demonstrate that small models can reach strong performance, and other studies[^3] investigate tool use to improve reliability. What those papers generally do not emphasize is reducing trace verbosity or explicitly training models to prefer short, computation-oriented traces executed in a constrained, auditable environment.

Offload deterministic computation to a safe executor.

Train models to prefer concise, computation-oriented traces over verbose text.

DeepMath tackles this by combining a small Python executor with a fine-tuned LLM, enabling concise, computation-driven reasoning. The model learns to generate short Python snippets, which are executed in a sandbox and reintegrated into the context. GRPO fine-tuning encourages this behavior by rewarding correctness and encouraging shorter outputs.

Figure 1: The vLLM client and server were modified to use the DeepMath agent in generating the candidates, while using the vLLM backend.

Agent Interface: During inference, the model can output normal tokens or special agent calls containing Python snippets.

Execution: Snippets run in a sandboxed environment with strict safety constraints (no file I/O, no network, timeouts).

Concision: Replace multi-line textual calculations with short, focused snippets.

Determinism & Safety: Enforce strict execution limits.

Interpretability: Snippets are readable and auditable.

Figure 2: Output example where python code is generated, evaluated and the answer is inserted into the trace and used for context.

We fine-tune the model using GRPO, a reward-based optimization that balances:

Using code snippets: +1 for generating code snippets, weighted 10:1 vs. the accuracy reward.

Length reduction: shorter lengths are encouraged by limiting the GRPO completion candidates to 5k tokens.

Temperature Scheduling: We implemented linear temperature scheduling (T=1.2 → T=0.7) to balance exploration and stability during training. This approach aims to enhance experimentation during the initial training phases, subsequently reducing the temperature as we refine our proficiency in the skill.

In-context Learning: we include 4 solved examples where the trace contains agent calls and executor outputs, so the model learns the syntax and the call/response pattern.

Dataset: we used the Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) subset of the OpenMathReasoning dataset. Note that GRPO only uses the problem, not the solution in the data. This dataset was chosen to ensure the problems benefit from the external tool.

We benchmarked DeepMath against baselines on four datasets. Metrics include:

majority@16: robustness across samples, as used in previous math reasoning works, see references.

We compare a baseline configuration (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, no agenting) with our DeepMath model. As ablation, we evaluate the agentic framework we developed running with the untrained Qwen3 model, denoted by +Agent. Additionally, we examine whether the GRPO training (for agentic use) improves non-agentic inference, denoted by +GRPO. Thus the two ablations are independent, not additive.

We observe the agentic inference reduces output lengths, with mixed accuracy results. The DeepMath model is both GRPO-trained and run in agentic mode, and shows the highest accuracy with shortened traces. We conclude both GRPO training and agentic inference are needed for best results.

Key Insight: DeepMath reduces output length by up to 66% while improving accuracy on challenging datasets.

Accuracy: Offloading computation reduces arithmetic errors.

Efficiency: Shorter outputs mean faster inference and easier interpretability.

Safety: Sandbox execution mitigates risks of running arbitrary code.

DeepMath demonstrates a practical and lightweight way to combine a small executor with an LLM and to train the model to prefer short, computation-driven traces. Offloading deterministic computation reduces arithmetic and numerical errors and shortens traces, and GRPO fine-tuning further encourages concise, correct answers. The result is a more accurate and more interpretable math-solving agent without requiring a massive model or heavyweight external tools.

Check out the GitHub repo and share your feedback! Contributions welcome. 🚀

If you use DeepMath in your research, please cite:

Scope: we focused on a small model and on mathematical reasoning.

Generalization: evaluated on contest-style math; results may not transfer to open-ended mathematical creativity or formal proofs.

Executing generated code is inherently risky. DeepMath uses strict sandboxing and resource limits, but any deployment should carefully manage attack surfaces and enforce rate limits.

#10394. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult

Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

We’ve added the basic white and black versions of the controllers above, but there are easily over a dozen versions of the G7 Pro spread out across over half a dozen listings on Amazon. Most of the basic color options (white, black, purple, etc.) are on sale for that $64 price. Some special versions, however, are more expensive. The new Sunset BLVD color, likely inspired by GTA VI, is $71.99, down from $89.99. The same is true of the AimLabs special edition.

Regardless of the version you go with, you get the same core features, including three replaceable D-pad options, microswitches on the face buttons and D-pad, analog triggers with either full motion or microswitch hair trigger, 8K polling when wired, TMR joysticks, and six-axis motion controls. It also comes with a dock that doubles as a charger and port for the 2.4 GHz wireless dongle. For devices that don’t support the dongle, such as a console, you can connect either wired or via Bluetooth. — Jake Roach

Both the Razer BlackShark V3 and its upgraded Pro variant are on sale for $50 on Amazon. Both the white and black versions of both headsets are eligible for the discount, though not the various collaborative models Razer has released for the BlackShark V3 Pro. We’re obviously linking the PC version of the BlackShark V3 Pro, but if you’re buying for a console, the PS5 and Xbox versions that give you 2.4 GHz wireless connection with your console are on sale, as well.

The Razer BlackShark V3 is a wireless headset that can connect via Bluetooth, USB-C, or a low-latency 2.4 GHz connection on PC.

The Razer BlackShark V3 Pro is a wireless gaming headset with Active Noise Cancellation (ANC). It support 3.5mm, Bluetooth, and 2.4GHz connections.

Both the V3 and V3 Pro are based on the same core design. They come with 50mm drivers, a detachable full-band microphone, Bluetooth, wired, and 2.4 GHz connections, and multi-device connection (including sound from one source and voice chat on another). That dual-source audio was a big selling point in our Razer BlackShark V3 Pro review.

The main addition with the Pro model is Active Noise Cancellation (ANC). At $200, the BlackShark V3 Pro headphones are fairly inexpensive for a pair of ANC cans, much less combined with a competitive-focused gaming headset. — Jake Roach

Despite Arrow Lake’s lackluster reputation, the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus is one of the best CPUs for gaming, and it’s our go-to recommendation for any non-gaming applications. Newegg has the CPU on an excellent deal right, knocking $70 off list price to bring the chip down to $250. On top of that, you get a free Rosewill 360mm AIO, as well as a game bundle that includes two codes of your choosing.

Get Intel's latest and greatest processor, the 270K Plus. The 8p/16e core processor has plenty of oomph to plow through any workflow and games well, too.

Our editor-in-chief Paul Alcorn just picked up this exact deal for his personal rig. Earlier this week, we saw the 270K Plus briefly drop down to $232, but that deal has long-since passed. You could argue this is a better pick given the bundled cooler and games.

The Core Ultra 7 270K Plus may only cost $250 on sale, but as you can see in the charts above, it offers flagship productivity performance and it’s within 10% of the gaming performance of AMD’s last-gen, but still coveted, Ryzen 7 7800X3D. Despite the Core Ultra 7 branding, this chip comes with 24 cores (8P + 16E), matching the more expensive Core Ultra 9 285K. In fact, in some applications, the 270K Plus is even faster due to boosted uncore frequencies. — Jake Roach

The Samsung P9 Express is our recommendation for the best budget 256GB MicroSD Express card for the Switch 2, and it’s on a stellar 44% discount right now on Amazon. Although not an all-time low due to flash prices shooting through the roof earlier this year, this is the lowest price we’ve seen on the 256GB P9 Express since March when flash prices started to climb.

A 256GB microSD Express card that offers sequential read speeds up to 800 MB/s and a three-year limited warranty.

This card has sequential read speeds up to 800 MB/s. As you can see in the charts below, the card fell squarely in the middle of the pack in our Mario Kart World test, and it reached 74 MB/s in our test transferring a game from the Switch 2 to the card. Of course, you don’t have to use this card with the Switch 2; it works with any standard microSD-card device.

Samsung backs up the card with a three-year warranty, which is a surprisingly long window given the budget price of the P9 Express. — Jake Roach

It’s not often you can get one of the best-performing PC components for less money than worse-performing alternatives. But that’s what you’ll be getting if you pick up Arctic’s Liquid Freezer III Pro 360, one of the best AIOs we’ve tested, for $65.99, or $71.99 for the RGB version.

This 360 mm AIO cooler delivers some of the best performance of any we’ve tested and supports recent Intel and AMD CPUs. It comes with four 120 mm (non-RGB) fans and even has a fan above the cooling block to lower the temps of your VRMs and RAM.

This 360 mm AIO cooler delivers some of the best performance of any we’ve tested and supports recent Intel and AMD CPUs. It comes with four 120 mm RGB fans and even has an RGB fan above the cooling block to lower the temps of your VRMs and RAM.

When we reviewed the Liquid Freezer III Pro in 2025, it was the best-performing AIO we’d ever tested, not only for pure thermal dissipation, but it was also one of the best when noise-normalized. And you will probably want to limit the pump and fan speeds, because this isn’t a quiet cooler when going full tilt. But you shouldn’t need everything this cooler can deliver unless you are chasing extreme overclocking records. This cooler is still our primary AIO pick, because nothing else has performed significantly better in this cooler's price range -- and that's when it's not on sale.

The only other real downside of this cooler is that Intel users will have to install a custom (included) contact frame, due to the way the cooler mounts. This isn’t a major hurdle, but it does complicate the installation process a bit, making this perhaps not the best CPU cooler for your first PC build. — Matt Safford

I’ve had this Anker hub plugged into my main PC’s top-panel USB-C port and stuck to the side of my case for a little over a year and it’s functioned flawlessly, letting me plug in storage devices, peripheral dongles and, of course, USB-C cables. It’s an easy way to turn one USB-C port into four, and put those ports where you need them.

This 3.31 × 1.85 × 0.55-inch hub has a permanently attached USB-C cable and four USB-C ports. They all deliver 10 Gbps data bandwidth, while one also handles DisplayPort for video up to 4K and PD charging passthrough, up to 100W.

It’s worth pointing out that several people have reported issues with video issues on Macs. But with my custom desktop and Lenovo laptop, I’ve had zero issues with this hub. It’s given me four USB-C ports at the front of my case, right where I need more connectivity. — Matt Safford

Taken at face value, the R8 mouse from 8BitDo is an ambidextrous mouse pulling at the strings of fond 8-bit memories. And its gray-on-gray color scheme and round red side buttons pull that part off well. But having owned and used it since March, for gaming and work, I can say it’s much more than that. The 26K optical sensor is more than enough for all but truly elite gamers. And the USB-C charging dock is nicer than what you’ll get with most mice that cost twice as much.

The nostalgia of this mouse's design is nice. But it also sports a 26,000 DPI sensor, 4K polling, and a really nice charging dock that also houses the 2.4 GHz dongle. If you're in a pinch or not gaming, Bluetooth is also supported.

I will admit that the round side buttons, which are slippery and slightly recessed, take some getting used to. But there are two on each edge, making the mouse truly ambidextrous. And after a couple of weeks using the M8 to play Borderlands 4 and Doom: The Dark Ages, I actually found that my fingers missed them when I switched to another mouse.

The rubber scroll wheel is ratcheted and pleasingly tactile. The only thing I don’t love about the design is that the very bottom of the mouse is a little sharp. But you only feel that when you pick it up to turn it on or off, switch from 2.4 GHz or Bluetooth, or to pair it.

I bought this mouse expecting it to be mostly about its looks, but it packs so much substance that I find myself using it more than gaming mice that cost much more. It also looks great next to the company’s NES-themed mechanical keyboard.

The Corsair Galleon 100 SD RGB is down to an all-time low price on Amazon. It's 26% off list price, bringing the $349.99 keyboard down to $259.99. The beats the previous all-time low by about $30.

This TKL mechanical keyboard features hot-swappable switches and a built-in Stream Deck with 12 LCD keys, a 2.75-inch screen, and 2 rotary knobs.

The Galleon 100 SD RGB is a full-sized keyboard, but instead of a numberpad, Corsair includes a 12-button Stream Deck, complete with a screen and two mappable knobs. On the 5-inch, 720 x 1280, you can monitor system sensors, check the time, see your playing music, and much more.

Thankfully, Corsair has a well-built keyboard to back up the flashy Stream Deck integration. It's a wired design with up to an 8,000Hz polling rate. For the sound and feel, Corsair uses a gasket mount with six layers of sound dampening. Out of the box, the keyboard uses Corsair's MLX Pulse switches, but the hot-swappable PCB is compatible with standard 3- and 5-pin switches. You can read more about the keyboard in our Corsair Galleon 100 SD review. — Jake Roach

For the MMOers among you — as well as the macro-everything crowd — you can grab Corsair Scimitar Elite Wireless SE for 50% on Best Buy right now. It comes with 16 programmable buttons, 12 of which are available in a grid for your thumb. The much-older Scimitar RGB Elite wired mouse is also on sale for 44%, bringing its price down to $49.99. Naturally, we recommend the newer, wireless Scimitar Elite Wireless SE for most people.

Corsair's wireless MMO / MOBA-focused gaming mouse features 16 programmable buttons, including 12 in a side array, and sports Corsair's 33K Marksman S optical sensor. It also has native integration with Elgato's Stream Deck platform, so you can map Stream Deck commands directly to the buttons.

The Scimitar RGB Elite mouse from Corsair features 17 programmable buttons, including 12 located on the side panel, the left/right primary mouse buttons, two DPI switch buttons above the scroll wheel, and the scroll wheel's center click. You can slide the 12-button side panel to fit your hand size.

As you can read in our Corsair Scimitar Elite Wireless SE review, the mouse comes with several upgrades over earlier Scimitar designs. It uses the same basic shape and button layout, but it comes with Corsair's 33K DPI Marksman S sensor, optical switches, and Stream Deck integration.

In addition to buttons and macros, you can bind the controls on the Scimitar Elite Wireless SE to Stream Deck functions, giving you a ton of flexibility in how you use the mouse. — Jake Roach

If you want chart-topping gaming and productivity performance in a single CPU, AMD's 16-core X3D chips are uncontested. They both provide gaming performance on-par with the Ryzen 7 9800X3D, top the charts in multithreaded productivity applications, and are in a close second place to Intel's Arrow Lake Refresh in single-threaded apps. Both CPUs are on deep discounts for Black Friday, with the dual-cache Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 hitting an all-time low at $759.

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 is AMD's first dual-CCD CPU with 3D V-Cache. It sports 16 cores and 192 MB of L3 cache, and it can boost up to 5.6 GHz.

The Ryzen 9 9950X3D features 128MB of L3 cache, which enables it to claim the title of the fastest gaming chip on the market. It features 16 Zen 5 cores and 32 threads of computing power, reaching a peak clock speed of 5.7 GHz.

Both CPUs feature 16 Zen 5 cores and 32 threads, along with AMD's stacked 3D V-Cache. The main difference is that the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 has that stacked across on both of its two CCDs, while the Ryzen 9 9950X3D only has the stacked cache on a single CCD. To accommodate the extra cache, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 also has a 100 MHz reduction in maximum boost clock, topping out at 5.6 GHz compared to 5.7 GHz on the 9950X3D.

In practice, the two chips perform identically in games, while the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 eeks out a small but measurable 4% improvement in multithreaded applications. For most people, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D is the better CPU, but if you want the best of the best, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 is on sale for an excellent price. — Jake Roach

If you’re anything like me who likes to know the intricate details of what’s going on with things, this 3.3-foot USB-C charging cable from UGreen and its LED display on one end should satisfy that itch. The cable supports up to 140W Max superfast charging (to 48V/5A) while the tiny screens display wattage, amperage, and voltage so you can see at a glance how much power the cable is passing.

If you're a techie like me and love to see the numbers behind what's going on, UGreen's 240W cable has a small LED display on the end that displays the wattage, voltage, and amperage going through the cable. This is great for just knowing or troubleshooting.

At $12.34, 46% off the list price, the cable is priced right and even supports data speeds up to 480 Mbps. The durable braided design resists tearing and is certified for 10,000 bend cycles. If you need a new cable, or just like the cool display, don’t pass up this Black Friday deal. – Joe Shields

There are a ton of excellent deals on controllers this Black Friday, even if you prefer something first party. The DualSense is on sale for $54 in a broad range of colors. Some of the more unique designs are more expensive, but they're on sale as well. For instance, the Rhythm Blue color is marked down from $84.99 to $64.

Sony's DualSense controller works natively with PC now, including features like Adaptive Triggers in supported games.

The controller works natively on PC, and although there are still some games without DualSense support, Steam Input allows you to use the controller with the vast majority of PC games without resorting to another app. You can pair it with your PC like another other controller via Bluetooth.

Some games have native DualSense support, which is where Sony's controller shines between its Adaptive Triggers and sharp haptic feedback system. Of course, Sony's first-party games support the DualSense on PC, but so do hundreds of other titles. — Jake Roach

The AudioEngine A2+ speakers have been our go-to recommendation for years on our roundup of the best PC speakers. The newer A2 GEN3 speakers have several improvements, including Bluetooth 5.4, adding support for various aptX codecs, and a Class D amplifier, which should help the speakers run cooler. AudioEngine also swapped out the micro-USB port on the original speakers for a USB-C port.

One of the best desktop speakers we've tested, now updated with USB-C and aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC for stellar wireless connectivity up to 100 feet, these are an excellent audio upgrade for any desk.

The cabinet and drivers remain unchanged. The speakers feature a 2.75-inch woofer and 0.75-inch tweeter, and they're among the best-sounding speakers in this class. They're expensive at $300, and even during shopping events, they don't always go on sale. That's what makes the 25% discount during Black Friday so attractive.

Outside of quality raw components, the speakers include a 24-bit internal DAC, and AudioEngine stands behind the speakers with a three-year warranty. — Jake Roach

If you’re always on the go with your laptop, it helps to have a power bank handy to keep your device charged without a wall outlet. Anker’s 25,000 mAh, 165W laptop power bank (model A1695) is a solid option. It’s now on sale at an all-time low of $91.19. The power bank sports an information LCD display that shows output wattage, percent left, and more.

Anker’s Laptop Power Bank is ideal for laptop users and features three 100W USB-C ports (two built-in, one retractable; the other doubles as a carry strap) and one Type-A for simultaneous charging up to 165W. It offers ultra-fast recharge speeds up to 100W with a compatible charger, plus a built-in screen to display charging information. It’s pricey, but it charges quickly and sustains its output over time in our testing.

Output includes two retractable Type-C cables, plus a Type-C port and a Type-A port, allowing you to charge up to four devices at once. It’s great for traveling and complies with 100Wh airline restrictions. If you’re looking for a powerful multi-port power bank, this Anker is one of the best deals for a high-quality device with a display. – Joe Shields

Given the current SSD market, it's been months since we've seen a drive at $0.10 per GB, but that's the price for this 2TB Silicon Power NVMe SSD. It's a PCIe 3.0 drive, so you're trading some speed for the price. However, it's still far faster than any SATA SSD, and many of those drives are selling for more than the cost of this one.

Perfect as a storage drive for your Steam library, this PCIe 3.0 drive can reach read/write speeds of up to 2200/1600 MB/s, respectively.

The drive comes with 2,200 MB/s and 1,600 MB/s sequential read/write performance. As you might expect, it's a DRAM-less SSD, instead relying on HMB and an SLC cache. It comes with an endurance rating of 1,200 TBW, which is excellent considering the price.

Although stepping down to PCIe 3.0 isn't ideal, there are a ton of applications for 2TB of storage where the slower speed won't matter much. Especially when looking at older games and media, the practical difference between this drive and even an expensive PCIe 5.0 isn't massive. — Jake Roach

UGreen’s X515 USB Wall Charger is only $9.44, a solid 43% (over $7) off the list price. We reviewed this charger and loved how cool it ran during our testing, as well as its efficiency. The small charger has two Type-C and one Type-A port for 30W total output. The X515 supports multiple charging protocols, including PD/QC 3.0, PPS, FCP, and AFC so you'll get the most out of most anything you want to charge.

The value pick in our low-wattage group is UGreen’s 3-port USB-C GaN II charger (X515). It's an affordable, high-quality option that supports charging multiple devices at once. It was among the most efficient chargers we tested, ran cooler than most of the competition, and was still compact enough for travel.

We named the X515 our low-wattage value pick in our Best Chargers article, beating several comparables. Overall, it’s a solid choice for anyone who needs a high-quality multi-port USB wall charger. And being well over 40% off makes this a steal for its class. – Joe Shields

SanDisk’s WD Black SN8100 clone, the 2TB Optimus GX Pro 8100 PCIe 5.0 SSD, is on sale for almost $95 off its typical price and at an all-time low, according to Amazon. For $349, you can get one of the faster 2TB drives. At less than $ 0.18 per GB, it’s one of the cheapest 2TB PCIe 5.0 drives available right now. The drive reaches speeds up to 14,900/14,000 MB/s (read/writes), nearly saturating PCIe 5.0 bandwidth.

Expand your internal storage with Sandisk's 2TB Optimus GX Pro 8100 PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSD. This speedy drive offers 14,900/14,000 r/w speeds and has a 5-year warranty.

Whether you use it as your primary OS drive or to store your most frequently accessed games, the SanDisk Optimus GX Pro 8100 2TB is an excellent option for a new PC or even upgrading your current storage. At an all-time low price of $349.99 (less than $0.18 per GB), it’s not only fast (faster than the Samsung 9100 Pro), but the price is right, too. – Joe Shields

It's all about speed. If you're streaming at 4K, or playing games online where latency can kill you before your opponents can, then you need fast networking. This TP-Link 5-port switch, down to just $7.99, can unlock an extra four gigabit Ethernet ports to your network for your PC, laptop, game consoles, and more.

All you need to do to use this unmanaged switch is to switch it on and hook it up to your router using one of the ports. If you're stuck with slow Wi-Fi, especially in a congested area, there isn't a better alternative. You'll be able to max out your internet connection's bandwidth with a faster wired network this way.

The TP-Link Litewave 5-Port Gigabit Ethernet Switch LS1005G provides four additional Ethernet ports, delivering reliable, high-speed wired internet for your gaming PC, NAS, console, TV, and other connected devices. Another popular Tom's Hardware recommendation and one that several of us own ourselves.

This is a plug-and-play option that doesn't need configuring, so it's perfect for a beginner and a pro. If you're struggling with lag or slow connectivity on your local network, then this $8 switch (along with some Ethernet cables) is an easy solution, and at a great price. — Ben Stockton

HP's HyperX gaming brand is known for its good quality peripherals, including gaming mics, which are easy to use and usually sound great. Right now, the HyperX SoloCast 2 is on sale, and it's down to just $44.98.

This USB condenser mic has just one polar pattern (cardioid); it's designed to pick up just one person's voice in front of it. It's well built, made of a solid black cylinder with a metal grille, weighing almost 13 ounces (365.7g). Unlike most mics, this has a built-in stand, which you can tilt back by around 40 degrees to angle it right at your face. It's backed with rubber at the bottom, too, so it won't slip around, with mounting points if you want to add it to a boom arm.

This 14mm electret condenser capsule mic features an integrated desktop stand that tilts the mic upward 40 degrees (there's a mounting point on the bottom of the stand, in case you do want to mount it on a boom arm). It has a cardioid polar pattern and sounds pretty good out of the box, and it features HyperX's signature tap-to-mute button on the top.

There's a USB-C port on the back, with a large tap-to-mute button on top for easy access, along with a red indicator light to let you know when you're muted. It records at a high-res 24-bit, 96 kHz bit-depth and sample rate, sounding very good out of the box. There's also a built-in internal shock mount and pop filter, although it's better mounted rather than sitting on your desk.

This HyperX mic is simple and a good starter option for a gamer or office worker, and thanks to the $44.98 sale price, it's cheaper than ever. You can check out our HyperX SoloCast 2 review to learn more. — Ben Stockton

Want to try out VR? Then Meta's budget-friendly Meta Quest 3S should enter your checkout. Thanks to Black Friday, it's on sale for just $297.49 right now at Newegg, a 15% price drop compared to its usual price. You're also scoring a $15 gift card that you can use to put towards another Newegg purchase.

The Meta Quest 3S is the most affordable VR headset from Meta. Despite that, it still comes with the same CPU, RAM, and base storage as the most expensive Meta Quest 3, while also offering a slightly better battery life.

The Meta Quest 3S is a completely wireless experience, so there aren't any cables or cords to worry about here, and you don't need a PC to power it. It's got a smaller battery compared to the Meta Quest 3, but this VR headset should still last for 2.5 hours with continuous use.

The controllers, meanwhile, are powered by a single alkaline AA battery each. It's probably worth keeping a few extra rechargeable lithium-ion batteries close at hand, though, so you don't get cut off mid-way through a game. The Meta Quest 3S would make for a great gift this holiday season, for yourself or for a loved one, especially with that 15% discount on top. — Ben Stockton

Another Black Friday deal is here for those audiophiles needing an upgrade to their desk audio setup. These Edifier M60 PC speakers are back down to $149.99 on Amazon right now. That's a $50 off the retail price and it brings it back down to record lows, a price we last saw during Amazon's October sale.

The Edifier M60 speakers come with 3-inch mid-low drivers and 1-inch tweeters, and they're relatively compact, measuring just 6.6 inches (168mm) high by 3.9 inches (100mm) wide. They come with a pair of aluminum speaker stands that angle the speakers up by 15 degrees, pointing them directly toward your ears when they're placed at a desk.

This pair of compact desktop stereo speakers features USB-C, AUX, and Bluetooth 5.3 connectivity, as well as touch controls and a built-in DSP. And they're on sale for their lowest price ever.

You can connect in a few different ways with the M60s, including by USB-C or traditional aux inputs, as well as by using Bluetooth 5.3. If you use Bluetooth, you can stream high-res audio (24-bit / 96 kHz) from mobile devices running Android 8 or later, too.

The speakers have a built-in DSP and touch controls that'll light up when you move your hand over them. With a total output power of 66W RMS, these aren't the most powerful PC speakers in the world, but they'll be a massive step up over listening through your laptop (or, worse, monitor's) tinny speakers. — Ben Stockton

There haven't been a huge amount of GPU deals during this Black Friday sales event, so this is a rare one. For $619, you can pick up this PowerColor RX 9070 GRE. It's the cheapest you'll find this GPU and, more importantly, it's a solid mid-tier performer for gaming at 1080p and 1440p at a far better price than rival GPUs like the RTX 5060 Ti.

This Radeon RX 9070 GRE is delivering great 1080p and 1440p gaming performance at a low price in today's market, giving you access to AMD's high-quality FSR 4 upscaler for a performance boost when you need it.

Our GPU hierarchy tests saw the RX 9070 GRE hit 90 FPS on average during all of our raster and ray tracing tests at 1080p, while also reaching 60 FPS at 1440p. Given the cost of this card, that's a really solid performance, especially as you might pay hundreds of dollars more for a rival Nvidia card to match it.

The 9070 GRE is an even better performer for pure raster gaming, hitting 120 FPS at 1080p and 90 FPS at 1440p, and that's before you even consider AMD's FSR 4 upscaling tech. If you want a quick, cheap and well-performing GPU upgrade for Black Friday, this PowerColor Reaper card might be one of the best ways to do it.

Dust: the enemy of all PCs. Dust is the perennial problem for PC owners, and once it builds up in your PC, it can cause it to overheat. Cleaning your rig regularly is the best course of action but, rather than rely on compressed air cans, you can invest in a compressed air duster, like this discounted Wolfbox MF50 for just $29.06, a new record low price for Black Friday.

An electric air duster, providing you with your own infinite supply of compressed air.

With this, you can banish the cans of compressed air and instead delete dust bunnies from your PC, along with any food or grime from your keyboard, along with any other areas of dirt collection on your desk. This portable and economical tool will keep your tech clean and tidy.

You can charge it over USB C in just 3.5 hours. It has a "turbo" fan that can reach speeds of up to 110,000 RPM, which provides up to four hours of use at its lowest setting. The MP50 has simple push controls, but all you really need to do is point and fire. There are four nozzles that'll help you control the airflow during a clean, too. — Ben Stockton

One of our favorite budget gaming chairs is now at an even better price for Black Friday. You can pick up the Razer Iskur V2 X for just $214.99 right now, a price drop of $85 compared to its usual list price.

The budget-friendly alternative to the Iskur V2, the Razer Iskur V2 X is a no-frills alternative that drives the price down by removing some of the adjustability options. That said, this chair still comes with built-in lumbar support, 2D armrests, and a 152-degree recline.

As our Razer Iskur V2 X review explains, this is the slightly less luxurious version of the OG Iskur V2. That does mean you have to accept a few compromises, but it's otherwise the same high-quality construction that we saw when we reviewed the original.

You're getting significant support on the base and back, high-density foam for the seat cushion, and adjustable 2D armrests here. Grab this steal of a Razer gaming chair at this price while you can. -- Ben Stockton

If you're traveling, you'll want a beefy portable power bank to fall back on to keep all of your devices charged. That's where this Ugreen Nexode 20,000 mAh power bank comes into play. It's on sale right now for $54.99, a new record low price that knocks $35 off the list price.

The UGREEN Nexode 20000 mAh power bank supports up to 130W of combined power output and features two USB-C and one USB-A port.

This power bank supports up to 100W of total power output across its two USB-C ports, but there's also a USB-A port for legacy devices that need charging. However, the different ports do have different max power levels: USB-C port 1 will give you 100W, while USB-C port 2 is capped at 65W, with the USB-A port at 22.5W max. According to Ugreen, this power bank can recharge a 13-inch MacBook Air up to 1.3 times if it's fully charged, or it can recharge an iPhone 16 Pro up to 3.7 times.

This Nexode bank also comes with a LCD display that'll tell you the current charge level of the battery, along with power output levels and the time remaining until the battery is discharged (or fully charged if it's charging). $54.99 for peace of mind while you're traveling isn't a bad option. — Ben Stockton

Power outages aren't fun, but they're especially not fun for your gaming PC. An outage can cause everything from lost data to electrical damage, but not if you buy this CyberPower UPS. It's on sale for $99.95 right now, a 29% price drop, bringing it down to a price we've not seen since 2023, according to Camelcamelcamel's price data.

This 900 V / 500 W battery backup protects up to six devices from a power outage, with a further six outlets offering surge protection. It has two USB charging ports.

This UPS battery pack is rated for 900 VA / 500 W and comes with 12 outlets. Six of them include both the battery backup protection, meaning you'll continue to have power after your electricity goes out, with an additional six offering just surge protection.

The pack also has spaced-out outlets for bigger plugs, along with two USB ports for charging. It has a three year warranty, along with a $125,000 guarantee to protect any devices you connect up to it. — Ben Stockton

Struggling with bad Wi-Fi? You need a router upgrade, and this TP-Link Archer BE550 for $149.99 is the answer, with a $100 saving to sink your teeth into. You're getting a ri-band Wi-Fi 7 router, able to provide up to 2,000 square feet of coverage, and fully expandable with EasyMesh-compatible devices.

You're able to get a combined maximum theoretical speed of 9.3 Gbps, split across the 6 GHz band for Wi-Fi 7, along with 5 and 2.4 GHz. If you're using a recent-enough device, Multi-Link Operation (or MLO) means you're able to use the different bands, like 5 GHz and 6 GHz, simultaneously for faster speeds and greater reliability.

The TP-Link Archer BE550 router packs six antennas, unlocking Wi-Fi 7 support for your network, with five 2.5 Gb Ethernet ports to help you future-proof your home network.

There are five 2.5 Gb Ethernet ports included in this BE550. One is the WAN port, so you'll use it to hook it up to your internet connection, along with four others that'll work for local devices like your gaming PC.

#10390. Build Live Video Chat With WebRTC: From First Call to Production Debugging

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money. Today every modern browser ships with WebRTC, a set of APIs that lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The catch is that WebRTC gives you building blocks, not a finished feature. This guide walks through those blocks in the order you actually need them, with the exact API calls you need, and then covers the production issues that tutorials usually skip.

A browser-to-browser call has four moving parts:

Start with the local preview. Browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS or localhost, so serve your page accordingly.

1.     Request a stream with navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(), passing video constraints (an ideal width of 1280 and height of 720 is a sensible default) and audio constraints with echoCancellation and noiseSuppression enabled.

2.     Assign the returned MediaStream to the srcObject property of your local video element.

3.     Keep a reference to the stream, because you will add its tracks to the peer connection later.

Set the muted and playsinline attributes on the local video element. Without muted users hear themselves, and without playsinline iOS Safari opens the video full screen.

The peers need a way to find each other. A tiny Node.js server using the ws package is enough for development. Its whole job is to relay messages between the peers in a room:

1.     Create a WebSocket server (for example with the ws package) listening on its own port.

2.     Keep a map of room names to the set of sockets in each room.

3.     When a client sends a join message, store the room name on the socket and add it to that room's set.

4.     For every other message type, forward the raw message to the other sockets in the same room, and never echo it back to the sender.

5.     On disconnect, remove the socket from its room so stale peers do not receive messages.

In production you would add authentication, limit room size to two for one-to-one calls, and validate message types, but the shape stays the same.

Both sides create an RTCPeerConnection, add their local tracks and listen for the remote ones:

1.     Create a new RTCPeerConnection with an iceServers list that contains at least one STUN server.

2.     Loop over the local stream's tracks and call addTrack() for each one.

3.     In the ontrack handler, attach the first remote stream to your remote video element.

4.     In the onicecandidate handler, send every new candidate to the other peer through your signalling channel as a candidate message.

One peer creates an offer, the other answers, and both apply each other's descriptions. Candidates arrive asynchronously in the background.

1.     The caller runs createOffer(), applies it with setLocalDescription() and sends the description as an offer message.

2.     The callee applies the offer with setRemoteDescription(), runs createAnswer(), applies it locally and sends it back as an answer.

3.     The caller applies the answer with setRemoteDescription().

4.     Both sides pass every incoming candidate message to addIceCandidate().

If both peers might start a call at the same time, look up the "perfect negotiation" pattern on MDN. It assigns one side as polite and resolves offer collisions cleanly instead of leaving both peers stuck.

On a home network, STUN alone often works. On corporate Wi-Fi, mobile carriers and symmetric NATs it frequently does not, and the call silently fails to connect. A TURN server relays media when a direct path is impossible. The open-source coturn server is the usual choice.

In practice, your iceServers list should contain your own STUN URL plus a TURN URL with a username and credential, so the browser can fall back to the relay automatically when direct connectivity fails.

Generate short-lived TURN credentials on your backend rather than hard-coding them, and budget for bandwidth: relayed calls pass every frame through your server.

Users deny camera access, unplug headsets and switch from Wi-Fi to 4G mid-call. Catch NotAllowedError and show a clear explanation, listen for devicechange events, and use RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack() to swap cameras without renegotiating the whole call.

Listen to pc.onconnectionstatechange. When the state becomes disconnected, wait a few seconds before giving up, because it often recovers. On failed, call pc.restartIce() to try new network paths.

Use RTCRtpSender.setParameters() to cap the bitrate on weak connections, and read pc.getStats() to monitor packet loss and round-trip time. Showing a small "poor connection" indicator does more for perceived quality than any codec tweak.

Mesh calls, where every participant connects to every other, work for two or three people. Beyond that, upload bandwidth explodes. Group calls need a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) such as mediasoup, LiveKit or Janus, which receives each stream once and forwards it to the others.

Tutorials end at a working demo, but the fastest way to understand what production WebRTC looks like is to watch a real call from the inside. Chrome ships an internal diagnostics page that shows every peer connection the browser opens, and it works on any site that uses WebRTC.

1.     Open chrome://webrtc-internals in one tab and keep it open.

2.     In another tab, start a call on your own demo and find its RTCPeerConnection entry.

3.     Expand that entry and look at the ICE candidate pairs: you will see whether the call went direct (host or srflx) or through a TURN relay (relay).

4.     Open the stats graphs for the outbound video stream and watch the bitrate, frame rate and resolution adapt when you throttle the network in DevTools.

5.     Check the negotiated codec and how quickly the connection recovers when you switch Wi-Fi off and back on.

Once you can read your own call, repeat the exercise on a production service. Any browser-based product works, whether a meeting tool or a live video chat that pairs two visitors, because webrtc-internals shows the same data for every site. Expect differences from your demo: more candidate pairs, a relay candidate in the list and a bitrate that adapts faster. Seeing them makes the earlier sections concrete, from why TURN matters to how bandwidth estimation reacts to packet loss.

The one-to-one call above is the core of many products, from telehealth consultations and tutoring to customer support. The engineering challenges grow with the use case: random matching needs queueing and presence on the signalling server, public platforms need moderation and reporting, and global audiences need TURN servers in several regions.

Start with the minimal version, get it working across Chrome, Firefox and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and add TURN before real users arrive. Once the call is reliable, every other feature becomes a much easier problem.

#10389. Introducing swift-huggingface: The Complete Swift Client for Hugging Face

Today, we're announcing swift-huggingface, a new Swift package that provides a complete client for the Hugging Face Hub.

You can start using it today as a standalone package, and it will soon integrate into swift-transformers as a replacement for its current HubApi implementation.

When we released swift-transformers 1.0 earlier this year, we heard loud and clear from the community:

swift-huggingface is a ground-up rewrite focused on reliability and developer experience. It provides:

One of the biggest improvements is how authentication works. The TokenProvider pattern makes it explicit where credentials come from:

The auto-detection follows the same conventions as the Python huggingface_hub library:

This means if you've already logged in with hf auth login, swift-huggingface will automatically find and use that token.

Building an app where users sign in with their Hugging Face account? swift-huggingface includes a complete OAuth 2.0 implementation:

The OAuth manager handles token storage in Keychain, automatic refresh, and secure sign-out. No more manual token management.

Downloading large models is now straightforward with proper progress tracking and resume support:

If a download is interrupted, you can resume it:

For downloading entire model repositories, downloadSnapshot handles everything:

The snapshot function tracks metadata for each file, so subsequent calls only download files that have changed.

Remember the second problem we mentioned? "No shared cache with the Python ecosystem." That's now solved.

swift-huggingface implements a Python-compatible cache structure that allows seamless sharing between Swift and Python clients:

The cache location follows the same environment variable conventions as Python:

To prevent race conditions when multiple processes access the same cache, swift-huggingface uses file locking (flock(2)).

Here's what downloading a model snapshot looked like with the old HubApi:

And here's the same operation with swift-huggingface:

The API is similar, but the implementation is completely different — built on URLSession download tasks with proper delegate handling, resume data support, and metadata tracking.

But wait, there's more! swift-huggingface contains a complete Hub client:

And that's not all! swift-huggingface has everything you need to interact with Hugging Face Inference Providers, giving your app instant access to hundreds of machine learning models, powered by world-class inference providers:

Check the README for a full list of everything that's supported.

Integration with swift-transformers. We have a pull request in progress to replace HubApi with swift-huggingface. This will bring reliable downloads to everyone using swift-transformers, mlx-swift-lm, and the broader ecosystem. If you maintain a Swift-based library or app and want help adopting swift-huggingface, reach out — we're happy to help.
