#10309. Elon Musk is giving away nearly $18 billion in SpaceX stock. Here’s who can get it

Your kid is becoming quite the capitalist.

Every U.S. child with an active Trump account will soon receive two shares of SpaceX, the space exploration company run by Elon Musk. This donation marks the latest in a string of philanthropic initiatives focused on these new types of tax-advantaged investment accounts.

SpaceX announced Wednesday that the company will donate one share of its Class A common stock—currently trading for more than $130 per share—to every currently active Trump account. In turn, CEO Musk will match that donation, which he later confirmed on X.

“Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally,” Musk posted. 

In its official announcement, SpaceX touted its future-focused mission of building new infrastructure that could achieve multiplanetary living. “We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit.”

Here’s what we know about the donations.

MILLIONS OF NEW SHAREHOLDERS

The portfolios of the country’s youngest generation of investors keep getting fatter. Launched earlier this year, Trump accounts allow deposits of up to $5,000 per year for each child until the age of 18 and various billionaires have even thrown some money into the mix.

Musk now joins the likes of Michael Dell and Ray Dalio, who have similarly pledged donations to Trump accounts. The U.S. Treasury Department, too, will make a one-time $1,000 deposit to every child born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028.

The SpaceX shares work a little differently in that the company will transfer one share of its stock to active Trump accounts in December, according to Musk’s post. Nearly 70 million accounts have been created thus far, the White House reported last month, though that’s largely a result of a change by the Treasury to allow for automatic enrollment. 

Musk’s matching donation will come later, he said on X, sometime after mid-June 2027. That’s when a 366-day lockup expires that he agreed to as part of the SpaceX initial public offering earlier this year.

The Starbase, Texas-based company noted that Gwynne Shotwell, its president and chief operating officer, previously pledged with her husband to donate more than 2 million shares to Trump accounts. But there are strict eligibility requirements associated with those donations, which parents can check online.

Combined, the gifts from the company, Musk, and Shotwell could have a value of more than $18 billion given the stock’s current price and if all eligible Trump accounts have been claimed. These donations also do something that’s delving into new territory: They guarantee that potentially millions of Americans will become long-term shareholders of SpaceX. 

YOU GET A STOCK!

Just as Oprah famously announced a new car to every person in her studio audience back in the early 2000s, Musk and other billionaires are saying the same to kids now: “You get a stock!”

But that could create a conundrum of sorts for parents as more and more money is likely to flow into these accounts from billionaires. 

The Treasury recently implemented new rules that allow companies and other donors to gift individual stocks to these accounts, while also limiting trading activity in them, as The Wall Street Journal reported. Children and their parents can neither pick nor reject stocks that are donated to a child’s account—and they can’t sell them for five years.

And yet, there’s free money on the line. If parents don’t claim an account on behalf of their kid, their kid misses out on a potentially lucrative portfolio. Despite the move to automatic enrollment, some manual steps are still required, which means parents need to claim an account by downloading an app from the Trump accounts website. 

Musk couldn’t help but tout the prospects of what that could mean to millions of prospective shareholders—something that resonated with investors, too, as the stock has jumped nearly 5% in the past two days of trading.

“If SpaceX succeeds in making life multiplanetary and harnessing even a millionth of the Sun’s energy, it will be worth about a million times the current global economy,” Musk posted. “These are obviously absurdly difficult goals, but there is a path to achieving them. I recommend holding on to your shares.”

#10308. Retail Merchandising Principles for Web Designers and Developers: Display Design, Ranking Rules and Measurement

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every e-commerce grid, product page and checkout screen is a shelf. Merchandisers have spent decades working out what to put at eye level, how many choices to show and how to tell whether a display works, and web teams are now rebuilding the same logic in code: sort orders, pinned products, badges, filters and A/B tests. Knowing where those ideas came from helps you build them with fewer mistakes.

This article maps physical retail merchandising onto digital product design. It covers visual hierarchy and choice load in listing UIs, a small rule-based ranking function you can test, accessible price and badge design with a contrast checker, and a significance test for layout experiments. It also covers why good plans fail at the handoff between design, engineering and operations. The numbers in the examples are illustrative, so use your own data. The code was run with Node.js 22.

Merchandising shapes how products are displayed, promoted and made accessible across sales channels. A well-planned strategy considers visual hierarchy, packaging, promotional materials, inventory timing and consistency between locations. For example, a skincare product may struggle to convert if testers are missing, shelf information is unclear or displays arrive after a campaign begins. If you build for the web, nearly every one of these problems has a direct counterpart:

Customers scan before they read. Nielsen Norman Group defines visual hierarchy as the arrangement of elements so the eye moves through them in order of importance, and names color and contrast, scale and grouping as the main tools. On a shelf, a larger facing or a contrasting background makes the hero product visible first. In a product grid, the equivalents are a larger card for a featured item, a clear boundary around a bundle, and a restrained use of badges so that only one or two items carry emphasis.

A common mistake is giving every card a badge, a color and a call to action. When everything is emphasized, nothing is, and the page reads like a crowded table in a store. Treat emphasis as a limited resource and have the design system say how many emphasized cards one screen may show.

A premium item placed beside entry-level alternatives may lose perceived value, and a crowded display can make fresh products look less appealing. Hick’s Law states that the time to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices, and its practical advice is to reduce options when speed matters and to highlight recommended ones. In a listing UI that suggests a curated first screen with a clear sort label, a few high-confidence recommendations and filters that handle the long tail, rather than an unbroken wall of products. Hick’s Law is a guide, not a rule, so treat it as a hypothesis to test on your own audience.

Merchandisers often ask for things like “pin the new range to the top, boost this collection, never show more than two items from one brand in a row, and push sold-out items down”. Implemented as scattered CSS order values and one-off queries, these requests become hard to audit. A small, pure function keeps the rules explicit and testable.

Because the function has no side effects, a short test can check every rule. This one confirms that pinned items lead, a pinned item that is out of stock is skipped, the brand cap pushes a third item from one brand behind other brands, sold-out items go last and a boost can lift a weaker product:

The design decision here is that stock demotion and the brand cap are defaults, while pins and boosts are inputs a merchandiser can change without a deploy, for example from a config file or admin screen. A real system would also log which rule moved each item, so that someone can answer why a product appears where it does.

Price cards and shelf labels are text, and text needs contrast. The WCAG contrast requirement asks for at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Product cards are a place where this slips, because grey secondary prices and pastel sale badges look refined in a mockup. The following script computes the WCAG contrast ratio, so you can run it over your design tokens in CI.

It prints 4.54 for mid grey #767676 on white, which just passes for normal text, 7.00 for #595959, which would also meet the stricter enhanced level, and 3.96 for the pink #d94f70, which fails for small badge text but would pass for large text. A sale badge that fails the check should be fixed in the token, not on one page.

A useful display respects the realities of the sales environment: floor space, customer movement, staff workload, replenishment access and how much information shoppers can absorb at a glance. The digital version is the gap between the design file and what ships. Test the setup with the people who will use it, not only with the team that created it, because their feedback reveals practical problems before a wide rollout.

A polished plan can fail in practice when materials arrive late, displays are assembled incorrectly or teams miss replenishment. On the web, the matching failures are a promotion that goes live before its product data is synced, a badge that stays on after a sale ends, and a hero banner that links to a discontinued item. Execution needs coordination across marketing, suppliers, logistics and engineering, with clear instructions, realistic schedules, display standards and checks. Some companies outsource this kind of field merchandising. One provider’s services page, for example, lists planogram and retail resets, end-cap displays, signage placement, on-shelf availability, in-store audits and visit reporting. Whether or not you hire help, that list is a useful checklist of what execution involves, and most items have a digital twin you can automate: availability checks, expiry dates on promotions and audit reports. Treat any performance figures on vendor pages as the vendor’s own claims and ask for evidence before relying on them.

Timing matters most for seasonal promotions and limited windows. A campaign that goes live after peak demand has passed cannot deliver the same value, so give promotional content a start and end date in the data model and have a scheduled job remove it, rather than relying on someone to remember.

Sales alone cannot tell you whether visibility, placement, stockouts, confusing information or poor setup caused a result. For a web listing, the answer is a controlled experiment. The script below compares conversion for a control grid and a variant with a two-proportion z-test, a standard way to check whether a difference is larger than chance would explain.

With these illustrative numbers, conversion rises from 3.00 percent to 3.90 percent, a relative lift of 30.0 percent, and the z value of 2.21 exceeds the 1.96 threshold for roughly 95 percent confidence. That does not prove the curated grid is better in general. It says this difference is unlikely to be noise for this test, and it assumes you fixed the sample size in advance and did not stop the moment the result looked good. Use a proper experimentation platform or a statistician for anything with real revenue at stake.

A strong merchandising operation does not require a large budget. A simple guide for product priorities, layout, pricing, replenishment and approved materials keeps execution consistent, and it is the physical version of a design system: a small set of approved components and rules that make the correct result the easy path. For a product card, that means a documented component with a fixed set of badge types, a defined maximum of emphasized items per screen and tokens that already pass the contrast check.

Consistency also protects trust. Damaged fixtures, inconsistent packaging, missing prices and outdated signs make good products look poorly managed, and the digital equivalents are broken images, stale prices and mismatched labels between the listing and the product page. Aim for consistency, not identical pages: a mobile grid and a kiosk screen can differ, but they should share product priorities, visual identity and core messages.

Temporary and in-store selling spaces demand quick communication. Visitors move fast, attention is limited, and interfaces must be clear from a distance and forgiving of mistakes. If you build kiosk, tablet or point-of-sale software, these constraints shape the interface:

When results disappoint, audit the real experience before commissioning a redesign. Think like a first-time customer: is the offer clear, are premium items distinct and can the team maintain the page easily? Government small-business guidance offers concrete analogues. The Queensland Government’s retail display guidance recommends showing essential information and prices so customers can decide quickly, placing popular or profitable items at eye level, and refreshing window displays every two to four weeks. The Westminster City Council guide similarly links visual merchandising, layout and planned promotions to attracting customers and encouraging them to spend more time and money in a business.

Prioritize visibility, clarity, stock accuracy and consistent execution before investing in a full redesign. Small operational improvements can make a meaningful difference, especially when they remove obstacles that repeatedly interrupt the buying process.

The public guidance cited here was written for general small-business use, and UX principles such as visual hierarchy and Hick’s Law come from interface research, so they are useful analogies rather than guarantees. The code is a teaching sketch: it ignores personalization, pagination, caching, search relevance and many other concerns of a production ranking system. Results vary with category, audience and device, so test changes in your own setting and treat any benchmark as a starting point.

What is merchandising in e-commerce? It is how products are displayed, ordered, promoted and made accessible across a site or app, including layout, labels, badges, sort rules and inventory handling.

How does visual hierarchy apply to a product grid? The same tools apply: contrast, scale and grouping decide what the eye sees first and which products read as related.

What should I measure first? Start with conversion, add-to-cart rate and stock availability for the listing, then add average order value and revenue per visitor once the basics are tracked.

How do I know a layout test is reliable? Fix the sample size in advance, randomize users, run it long enough to cover weekly patterns and check significance, for example with the two-proportion test above.

Do small teams need a big design system? No. A short component guide with a few badge types, spacing rules and accessible color tokens is enough to keep pages consistent.

Merchandising is applied interface design with a long history. Clear hierarchy, a curated first screen, readable prices, explicit ranking rules and controlled experiments carry over directly from the shelf to the screen. For designers and developers, the practical lesson is that a good layout only counts if it ships correctly, stays current and is measured. Audit the basics, put the rules in code, test one change at a time and record what you learn.

#10307. Hands-on: Sony’s Walkman-revival USB-C headphones are back in stock and worth a look

Sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after quickly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked. And, after using them, I can see why they sold out so quickly.

The MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player. The retro style still looks great in 2026, but using an original pair is a bit of a headache in today’s age of headphone jack-less smartphones. So it was nice to see Sony give this a revival with USB-C.

Update 11/24: After we first published our hands-on with MDR-3R last week, Sony’s USB-C headphones sold out pretty quickly again. As of today, though, they’re back in stock and still shipping in early December – don’t miss out!

While the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly. The sound quality is excellent and having a pair of headphones that doesn’t fully enclose my ears is pretty refreshing. There’s no noise cancellation, but with open-ear earbuds becoming more popular, I actually really like these as a similar solution (though high volumes will definitely be heard by those around you). I’m not fully cut off from the world around me, but I’m also able to get good sound quality. Lows are the weakness here, with unimpressive bass drops, but the sound quality is crisp and clear and pretty neutral, and the open-ish style makes it feel like the room around me is filled with music.

The physical hardware is great. While a plastic and metal build is objectively not as comfy as a premium pair of ANC headphones, the extremely light weight helps MDR-3R become an afterthought. You simply forget you’re wearing them after a few minutes.

The earpads are swappable, with orange and blue options included in the box.

As for the USB-C cable, it’s fully plug-and-play. No app needed and it worked across every device I tested (including Pixel, which doesn’t work with all USB-C audio output). I do wish the cable was perhaps a few inches longer, but it’s long enough to wear the headphones with my phone in my front pocket. There’s a remote along the cable for play/pause and volume adjustments, though I think it’s a little too high on the cable.

For $59.99, these are a fun pair of USB-C headphones to have on hand. They sound good, work great, and don’t cost an arm and a leg. I can see why they sold out so quickly on launch day – in just 10 hours, Sony told me.

Sony MDR-3R are back in stock now and shipping in early December. If you want a pair, I say don’t wait. They’re well worth at least trying if you can get them for retail price – please don’t give in to the scalpers selling these at double, they’re not worth that.

#10305. A popular password manager was hacked. Here’s what you need to know

Password managers are the safest way short of secret sticky notes to keep track of the hundreds of logins in your life, but even they don’t have perfect security.

Popular Password manager 1Password disclosed this week that hackers breached its systems this month and accessed the software’s source code. While no breach is good news, the attackers were not able to access 1Password users’ most sensitive data, including their passwords, secret keys, and information stored in user vaults. 

“At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” the company emphasized in a blog post on the incident. The security of the software maker’s apps and browser extensions was also not affected by the breach.

The attackers were able to burrow into 1Password’s system after gaining access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. By pushing malicious code into its backend systems, the attackers made off with administrative data on a subset of 1Password customers, including customer names, email addresses, and “non-secret internal metadata” about accounts. 

Anyone who uses 1Password doesn’t need to take extra steps right now, but they should be extra vigilant for phishing attempts in the future. That includes being skeptical of “unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts,” according to the company. The password manager will never ask its customers for an account password or a secret key.

In response, 1Password says that it has disabled the compromised GitHub account, rotated and revoked exposed internal credentials, and brought in external cybersecurity experts to advise the software maker on its response, among other measures.

Security for everybody

The world of cybersecurity moves fast – and now that cycle is speeding up even in light of AI. Security companies are leveraging artificial intelligence to detect threats at the same time that malicious actors are putting it to work cracking into accounts at scale.

1Password CTO Nancy Wang described the unique challenges and opportunities the company faces in light of widespread AI adoption in a recent interview with Fast Company. While a sea of vibe-coded apps have introduced security holes human software makers would have caught, AI can also scan massive chunks of code for vulnerabilities. “AI’s been a mixed bag, just because that work has been so gnarly and technical,” Wang said.

Aside from the millions of people who rely on 1Password, more than 200,000 businesses use the password manager to keep track of their credentials. That number includes nearly a third of the largest companies in the U.S., according to 1Password. Fast Company named the software maker to its 2025 list of Brands That Matter for its user-friendly approach to security. 

“1Password was built on the belief that security should be accessible to everyone,” 1Password CEO David Faugno said last year. “In an industry that too often leads with fear and complexity, we’ve built our foundation on trust, usability, and the human experience.”

#10304. The 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade isn’t canceled. Here’s when you can watch it this weekend

Thanksgiving may be over, but one of the holiday’s biggest traditions is still to come.

For the first time in its history, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is taking place on a day other than Thanksgiving. On Wednesday, Macy’s, NBC, and New York City officials made the unprecedented decision to postpone the parade until Saturday, November 28, after forecasts called for dangerous winds, heavy rain, and coastal flooding.

While the parade was canceled from 1942 through 1944 during World War II, weather has never before forced organizers to move the event to another day.

The timing is particularly noteworthy given that this year marks the parade’s 100th edition, a milestone Macy’s is celebrating with an expanded lineup of balloons, floats, musical performances, and celebrity appearances.

NBC aired a replay of the 2025 parade on Thanksgiving morning instead. The live celebration will take place Saturday, although the last-minute schedule change has forced some performers to adjust their plans.

Here’s what to expect from the rescheduled parade and how to watch it.

Who is performing at the 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade?

Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb, and Al Roker are slated to return as hosts of NBC’s broadcast.

The originally announced musical lineup includes RAYE, Teddy Swims, Megan Moroney, Natasha Bedingfield, Queen Latifah, Jimmy Fallon and The Roots, JoJo, Smash Mouth, and Keke Palmer, among others.

A special Broadway performance featuring a 10-minute medley from nine musicals, including Hamilton, Wicked, and Rent, is still expected to take place. The Radio City Rockettes are also on the announced lineup.

However, not everyone who planned to participate on Thursday will be able to stick around for Saturday.

The University of Alabama’s Million Dollar Band, for instance, is returning home to perform at Saturday’s Iron Bowl football game. Macy’s Great American Marching Band is also unable to participate in the rescheduled event.

Other groups have turned to crowdfunding to cover the unexpected cost of extending their stays in New York. A high school marching band from Pearland, Texas, raised $350,000 in less than 24 hours to enable more than 500 students and staff members to stay for the parade.

How to watch the 2026 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade

The rescheduled parade will step off at 8:30 a.m. ET on Saturday, November 28, and is expected to conclude around noon.

NBC will televise the parade, while cord-cutters can stream it on Peacock. A Spanish-language broadcast will also be available on Telemundo. Viewers with live TV streaming subscriptions that carry NBC, including YouTube TV, Hulu + Live TV, and Fubo, can also tune in.

If you’d rather sleep in on Saturday morning, NBC is scheduled to air an encore presentation at 2 p.m. ET/PT.

#10302. Alyah ⭐️: Toward Robust Evaluation of Emirati Dialect Capabilities in Arabic LLMs

📦 Dataset on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub

Arabic is one of the most widely spoken languages in the world, with hundreds of millions of speakers across more than twenty countries. Despite this global reach, Arabic is not a monolithic language. Modern Standard Arabic coexists with a rich landscape of regional dialects that differ significantly in vocabulary, syntax, phonology, and cultural grounding. These dialects are the primary medium of daily communication, oral storytelling, poetry, and social interaction. However, most existing benchmarks for Arabic large language models focus almost exclusively on Modern Standard Arabic, leaving dialectal Arabic largely under-evaluated and under-represented.

This gap is particularly problematic as large language models increasingly interact with users in informal, culturally grounded, and conversational settings. A model that performs well on formal newswire text may still fail to understand a greeting, an idiomatic expression, or a short anecdote expressed in a local dialect. To address this limitation, our team introduces Alyah الياه (which means North Star ⭐️ in Emirati), an Emirati-centric benchmark designed to assess how well Arabic LLMs capture the linguistic, cultural, and pragmatic aspects of the Emirati dialect.

The Emirati dialect is deeply intertwined with local culture, heritage, and history. It appears in everyday greetings, oral poetry, proverbs, folk narratives, and expressions whose meanings cannot be inferred through literal translation alone. Our benchmark is intentionally designed to probe this depth. Rather than testing surface-level lexical knowledge, it challenges models on their ability to interpret culturally embedded meaning, pragmatic usage, and dialect-specific nuances.

The benchmark covers a wide range of content, including common and uncommon local expressions, culturally grounded greetings, short anecdotes, heritage-related questions, and references to Emirati poetry. The goal is not only to measure correctness, but also to understand where models systematically succeed or fail when confronted with authentic Emirati language use.

Following further development and consolidation, the benchmark has been unified into a single dataset called Alyah. The final benchmark contains 1,173 samples, all collected manually from native Emirati speakers to ensure linguistic authenticity and cultural grounding. This manual curation step was essential to capture expressions, meanings, and usages that are rarely documented in written resources and are difficult to infer from Modern Standard Arabic alone.

Each sample is formulated as a multiple-choice question with four candidate answers, exactly one of which is correct. Large language models were used to synthetically generate the distractor choices, after which they were reviewed to ensure plausibility and semantic closeness to the correct answer. To avoid positional bias during evaluation, the index of the correct answer follows a randomized distribution across the dataset. Below is the distribution of word count per query and candidate answers.

Alyah spans a broad spectrum of linguistic and cultural phenomena in the Emirati dialect, ranging from everyday expressions to culturally sensitive and figurative language. The distribution across categories is summarized below.

This composition allows Alyah to jointly evaluate surface-level conversational fluency and deeper cultural, semantic, and pragmatic understanding, with a particular emphasis on dialect-specific language phenomena that remain challenging for current models.

We evaluated a total of 54 language models, comprising 23 base models and 31 instruction-tuned models, spanning several architectural and training paradigms. These include Arabic-native LLMs such as Jais and Allam, multilingual models with strong Arabic support such as Qwen and LLaMA, and adapted or regionally specialized models such as Fanar and AceGPT. For each family, both base and instruction-tuned variants were evaluated in order to understand the impact of alignment and instruction tuning on dialectal performance.

All models were evaluated under a consistent prompting and scoring protocol. Responses were assessed for semantic correctness and appropriateness with respect to Emirati usage, rather than literal overlap with a reference answer. This is particularly important for dialectal evaluation, where multiple valid phrasings may exist.

For each question category, we estimated difficulty empirically based on model performance. Categories where most models struggled were labeled as harder, while those consistently answered correctly across model families were considered easier. This approach allows difficulty to emerge from observed behavior rather than from subjective annotation alone.

We evaluate a broad set of contemporary Arabic and multilingual large language models on Alyah, using accuracy on multiple-choice questions as the primary metric. The evaluation covers 53 models in total, including 22 base models and 31 instruction-tuned models, spanning Arabic-native, multilingual, and regionally adapted systems. Below is a radar plot showing the performance of top models of different sizes per question category.

These results are intended as reference measurements within the scope of Alyah, rather than absolute rankings across all Arabic benchmarks.

Several trends emerge from the evaluation. Instruction-tuned models generally outperform their base counterparts as shown in Figures 1 and 2. This is particularly the case on questions involving conversational norms and culturally appropriate responses (i.e. the Etiquette & Values Category). Furthermore, it is the case with questions that test imagery and figurative meaning. This can be attributed, to the model’s original strong capabilities with understanding MSA-based imagery and figurative language regardless of the dialect at hand. The models are able to draw patterns of non-literal description regardless of dialect. Generally, the most difficult categories for the models were consistently “Language and Dialect” and “Greeting and Daily expressions” across model sizes as shown in figure 1. These results reflect the current state of Emirati dialect presence in written media, as the dialect is mostly spoken rarely written, which explains its novelty relative to the evaluated models. Nonetheless, there is a clear benefit to instruct models with understanding the dialect (and the other evaluation categories) in comparison to their counterparts, especially in small and medium models. This is particularly noticeable with the Poetry and Creative Expression category, which is where the large instruct models performed marginally better than the smaller models.

As shown in Figure 3, even strong multilingual models show notable degradation on the most challenging Alyah questions, suggesting that dialect-specific semantic knowledge is not easily acquired through generic multilingual training alone. It must be noted that while Arabic-native models tend to perform more robustly on culturally grounded content, their performances are not uniform across all categories (figure 2). In particular, questions involving implicit meanings and rare expressions remain difficult across nearly all evaluated models. This highlights a persistent gap between surface-level dialect familiarity and deeper cultural understanding. The high variance in performance across categories , where a model that excels at imagery and figurative meaning may still struggle with poetry or heritage-related creative questions, indicates that dialectal competence is multi-dimensional and cannot be captured by a single score. Figure 3 shows that the highest scoring large model in Jais-2-70B, followed by the two small models jais-2-8B and ALLaM-7B-instruct, which are all Arabic instruct-tuned models.

This benchmark represents a step toward more realistic and culturally grounded evaluation of Arabic language models. By focusing on the Emirati dialect, we aim to support the development of models that better serve local communities, institutions, and users in the UAE. Beyond model ranking, the benchmark is intended as a diagnostic tool to guide future data collection, training, and adaptation efforts.

We invite researchers, practitioners, and the broader community to use the benchmark, explore the results, and share feedback. Community input will be essential to refining the dataset, expanding coverage, and ensuring that dialectal Arabic receives the attention it deserves in the evaluation of Large Language Models.

#10300. The 4 secret Amazon clearance sites you should check before buying retail

As we power toward the holidays, the shopping pressure is officially on. Your natural instinct may be to type what you need into the Amazon search bar, click the first Prime-eligible result, and pay whatever price the algorithm spits out. That’s a huge mistake.

Amazon buries its best discounts on purpose. The retail giant operates three distinct clearance portals where you can score open-box electronics, overstocked gifts, and refurbished tech for up to 70% off retail. Before you pay full price for holiday gifts this year, here’s where you actually need to look.

Amazon Resale

Formerly known as Amazon Warehouse, Amazon Resale is where Amazon sends customer returns. The trick to using Resale is understanding its strict grading system.

If you buy an item rated as Used—Like New, it means the product itself is in perfect, untouched condition, but the original shrink wrap is broken or the cardboard box has a minor dent.

You get a massive discount simply because the packaging isn’t pretty enough to sit on a retail shelf. If you’re buying tech gear or kitchen appliances where the box just goes straight into the recycling bin anyway, it’s the easiest way to save hundreds. Just stick strictly to the Like New or Very Good tiers.

Amazon Outlet

Unlike Resale, everything in Amazon Outlet is brand new. This is where Amazon dumps seasonal overstock and excess inventory that’s taking up too much physical space in its fulfillment centers.

Finding it is the hard part. It isn’t advertised on the home page. You have to type amazon.com/outlet directly into your browser or dig deep through the Deals and Savings menu on the mobile app.

Once you’re in, you’ll find everything from holiday decorations to winter apparel marked down by 50% to 70%. It’s the absolute best spot to hunt for stocking stuffers and white elephant gifts without breaking the bank.

Woot

Amazon bought Woot back in 2010, but it still operates as a standalone site at woot.com. It’s a dedicated daily deal platform that runs flash sales on electronics, tools, and apparel until the inventory sells out.

If you’re hunting for a refurbished television, a discounted sound bar, or cheap smart home gear, Woot should be your first stop every morning. The checkout system is fully integrated, meaning your Prime membership still gets you free shipping. Just be prepared to act fast, because the best tech deals usually vanish before your morning coffee gets cold.

Amazon Haul

If you’ve ever been tempted to buy cheap stocking stuffers off Temu or Shein but didn’t want to hand your credit card to an overseas app, you’ll be interested to know that Amazon built a direct competitor right inside its own ecosystem.

It’s called Amazon Haul, and the gimmick is simple: Every item comes from outside the U.S., which often means cheaper, direct-from-manufacturer pricing.

Free shipping kicks in once you hit $25; less than that, and there’s a $4 shipping charge per order. While you lose next-day delivery—items can take up to a couple of weeks to arrive—and the return window drops to just 15 days, every purchase is still backed by Amazon. That makes it a safer way to buy ultra-cheap phone cases, kitchen gadgets, and holiday party supplies without risking a scam.

Last week, Google announced that Gemini tasks (previously called Spark) is now available to free users in the US, along with an integration in Google Messages. In testing, I’ve found this instance of Gemini to be proactive and feel more like an assistant than the Gemini app does.

The original Gemini integration in Google Messages dates back to 2024 with a dedicated FAB (floating action button) above Start chat. It lets you have a straightforward conversation with Gemini.

This updated experience makes use of the “Channels” feature introduced last week that allows you to Text or Email with Gemini to accomplish tasks.

With the latest Google Messages beta (version 20261120_01_RC00), we’re seeing the Gemini FAB (or top-right corner icon with the homepage redesign) open gemini.google.com/channels on a fresh install. If you’ve already set up the new integration, the shortcut takes you to the new chat, which uses RCS Business Messaging behind the scenes.

After using it for the past few days, the proactive nature of Gemini tasks in Google Messages has really stood out. Every morning, Gemini messages me about what’s on my schedule or what should be on my radar. Examples include:

While this instance of Gemini is ostensibly for tasks, I’ve been able to ask general knowledge questions, like about the weather, similar to the old experience. Additionally, you can upload attachments like images and files.

This new Google Messages integration is currently available in the US and requires that you have tasks enabled in the Gemini app.

#10298. 5 AI Tools for Creating Audio-Led Music Videos: A Practical Workflow

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

You can open on the singer’s first line, cut to another image as the instruments answer, and return to the singer for the key line of the chorus. If that return depends on a convincing close-up, test it before building the rest of the video. Choose a phrase with a quick consonant followed by a held vowel. Those two sounds give you clear points to check against the recorded vocal.

Use the recorded vocal as the timing reference. AI tools can help build opening shots, instrumental cutaways, and singing performances. Compare MakeSong, HeyGen, and Hedra on the singing shots themselves, and try Freebeat for an audio-led visual draft.

For creators developing multimedia experiences, the workflow also connects with broader web technologies. SitePoint's guide to building better video experiences on the web explores some of the practical considerations involved in working with video content.

AISong provides an image-led way to build the visual world around a recorded track. It fits a performance video that uses atmosphere and supporting shots in addition to views of the singer.

AISong’s AI Music Video Generator combines the song with a set of image references for a multi-shot sequence. Use that feature for the opening, an instrumental cutaway, or an establishing scene that can support the performance footage. Check whether the setting and the singer’s close-up look like they belong in the same video.

When preparing these assets for a website or multimedia project, consistency between images and video clips is important. This is also relevant to the process of building an AI media pipeline from concept art to web video.

Portrait art, rehearsal stills, or images of the setting can give these supporting shots an established look. It is particularly useful when some parts of the song call for visuals that give the audience a break from the performer.

MakeSong can build a video around the recorded track and reference images. Its lip-sync option requires a real human face. Start with a clear frontal image and check the result against the original vocal.

MakeSong’s AI Music Video Generator accepts audio, images, and a written prompt. The product page also offers lip sync for eligible face references. Give the close-up a particular vocal phrase and reserve a wider shot for the next musical response. Check mouth timing and the performer’s appearance at the cut.

This approach works when a single visual brief needs to connect the performance with the supporting scenes. The artist should have an approved reference and a clear idea of when the singer should appear.

HeyGen is a performer-led music video option. It is particularly relevant when the same on-screen singer should remain recognizable through more than one setting or camera distance.

Its music video workflow accepts a song and supports singing performance. Use a close and a wider view to compare mouth timing and continuity on the same vocal phrase. Watch for changes in the face or outfit when the framing shifts.

Choose this route when viewers need to follow the same singer across several scenes. This makes more sense than a single avatar clip when the performer is the visual thread for the whole video.

Hedra can animate a portrait from an audio clip. Try a single line with a quick consonant followed by a held vowel to see where the mouth falls behind the recording.

A clear portrait and one clean line give you a controlled test. Inspect the start and end of the phrase, then check how the clip cuts to the next shot. When only one line is convincing, use that line and let the original edit carry the rest.

A short close-up or a fictional singer’s entrance in the chorus is a good use for this approach. It is a practical fit when you already have an edit and only need one additional vocal moment.

Freebeat offers an audio-to-video workflow with a performance-oriented mode. It gives artists another way to test a performance cut driven by an uploaded track.

Use its singing video route for an excerpt with an audible pause and a clear vocal re-entry. Compare whether the performance feels natural during the pause and whether the visual action resumes where the vocal does. Keep the same approved track for the comparison.

Try this early to compare a full performance treatment with a version built from shorter clips before settling on an edit.

Decide how much of the release the singer needs to carry. An image-led sequence can support the track around key lines, a performer-led workflow can keep the singer present through the full edit, and an avatar clip can cover a single important phrase.

For developers and designers working with audio and video on the web, the final production stage also deserves attention. Video formats, playback behavior, and audio synchronization can affect how the finished content performs across devices. SitePoint's tutorial on the Web Audio API provides useful background on handling audio in web applications.

Judge the hardest line first and use the original vocal as the reference at every cut. Once the performance works, build the supporting shots around it and prepare the final video for its intended platform.
